But crown prosecutor Brett Hatfield SC urged the jury to reject Lamarre-Condon’s account and convict him on all three counts, as he finished his closing statement on Monday.
“The case is that the accused, driven by this jealous obsession, drove to Paddington in a hire car, scoped the house and waited for his opportunity,” he told the court.
Lamarre-Condon entered the house with a gun loaded with stolen bullets, and shot Baird in the back and temple, Hatfield alleged.
“It was not self-defence or an accident,” he said. “The evidence speaks only to an execution.”
Lamarre-Condon had testified he shot Baird after he lunged at him with a knife.
During this struggle, his gun was then flung across the room and picked up by Davies before the officer grabbed his arm and pushed the gun towards Davies.
Davies then pulled the trigger and shot himself, Lamarre-Condon told the court.
But this defence rests entirely on his own account and even if Baird had picked up a knife, it would not have assisted him against a Glock pistol, Hatfield said.
“You might think he is a proven and persistent liar and such a scenario is completely contrary to the weight of the evidence,” he told the court.
“The accused’s account is not the truth. It is a story made up after the fact in an attempt to meet the evidence.”
But Stratton said there were two serious problems with the crown case about Davies’ death that the prosecution “hasn’t overcome and can never overcome”.
Though Davies’ DNA was found on the trigger of the gun, there was no blood, the jury heard.
Davies being the source of the majority of DNA on this part of the gun is “powerful” evidence his finger was on the trigger when the third shot was fired, Stratton said.
The prosecution also failed to locate the bullet or any bullet fragments of the shot that struck Davies, and this is enough to leave jurors with reasonable doubt about the crown case, the barrister said.
“The forensic and ballistic evidence makes it more likely that the accused’s version is true, than the version the crown seeks to persuade,” he told the court.
The trial before Justice Natalie Adams continues.

title: ‘Difficult geopolitical times’: Albanese defends Bowen after Cop31 deal failure
text:
Anthony Albanese has defended Chris Bowen from criticism following the failure of the UN Cop31 climate summit, blaming the result on “difficult geopolitical times” as the Coalition called for the minister to resign.
Bowen served as president of negotiations at the talks in Turkey, helping run the conference with his Turkish counterpart, Murat Kurum.
Speaking to journalists late on Sunday after a list of countries rejected a proposed “cover decision” – an overarching agreement – for the conference, Bowen said “Australia left nothing on the field” but the “red lines” he and his staff tried to negotiate to find consensus between nearly 200 countries were unbridgeable.
The biggest sticking point was whether the agreement would mention the need for the world to transition away from fossil fuels. The European Union, Panama, the Marshall Islands, Vanuatu, Norway and Belize told the conference they would not accept a deal without it.
Saudi Arabia and Russia led a group of oil-rich countries that vowed to veto a decision that included mention of fossil fuels.
Bowen told reporters: “I would have been happy with [a] transition away from fossil fuels being in the text, but that was not going to get support.”
He said despite the breakdown, “in the real world” the transition away from fossil fuels was inevitable and happening at speed. He said more than 90 countries had signed a pledge to increase electrification to 35% by 2035 – a step that should help cut fossil fuel use if delivered – but acknowledged the result was “very disappointing”.
Australia was sharply criticised during the conference for its continued support for new coal and gas export developments. Speaking on Monday, Albanese said Australia’s efforts had been critical in building relationships with Pacific neighbours.
“It’s evidence that we’re living in difficult geopolitical times,” he said of the result. “That is the reality. The important work of Cop is the work that we’ve done with the Pacific, where Australia and our Pacific leaders have worked constructively together.
“In order to have credibility [in the Pacific], the entry fee is action on climate change.”
The Coalition’s energy spokesperson, Dan Tehan, said Bowen should “resign immediately”.
“If Chris Bowen does not resign immediately, the prime minister should sack him,” Tehan said. “As the lead negotiator, Chris Bowen is personally responsible for this catastrophic diplomatic disaster.”
The Greens’ deputy leader, Steph Hodgins-May, said it was a “disastrous embarrassment” that Australia had chaired negotiations over the failed deal. In a statement, she said Labor was “not fit to lead – not on the world stage for climate negotiations, and not at home when it comes to protecting Australians from climate destruction”.
The Coalition, and Tehan specifically, have consistently attacked Labor’s bid to host the conference and Bowen’s installation as president of negotiations. Bowen argued for the role – newly created for Cop31 – after Turkey won the hosting rights after a protracted stand0ff.
Tehan did not say what the Coalition would have done differently if he was in Bowen’s shoes, other than saying the opposition would not have pursued hosting Cop or the position of president of negotiations. The Coalition has abandoned its support for Australia reaching net zero emissions by 2050 – a target introduced under former Liberal prime minister Scott Morrison – and promised to abolish Labor’s climate policies if elected.
It has not put forward any policies to reduce emissions.
Tehan said the consensus model of agreement used at the UN summit was “completely and utterly broken”. “Chris Bowen should have known that,” he said.
While the failure to get countries to agree to the “Antalya pact” in Turkey was a significant moment in the history of UN climate summits, the talks did not collapse completely.
The sticking point was the attempt to find language to reflect the “transition away for fossil fuels” that had been agreed to in 2023 in Dubai.
In the final stages of the talks, countries were presented with a text that only referred back to that decision and did not explicitly say “fossil fuels” – infuriating a sweep of countries.
Bill Hare, the Australian chief executive of Climate Analytics and a Cop veteran, said the lack of agreement on the main document at Cop31 – there was consensus on some minor issues – should not be seen as a failure of the entire Cop process but as “a successful defence of the [UN climate convention’s] integrity against a coordinated attack by a few countries implacably opposed to action on climate change, in particular to any mention of the need to transition away from fossil fuels”.
Amanda Cahill, founder of the Next Economy, was in Antalya to offer advice on elements of the conference dealing with the so-called “just transition” – a wide-reaching set of guidelines meant to protect communities and workers affected by climate change and the shift away from the fossil fuel industry.
“While we didn’t get the outcome we wanted at this Cop, we maintained the global commitment to justice and equity as countries transition their economies to deal with climate change,” she said.
“We’ve got a lot of work ahead of us, but parties have committed to ensuring the Just Transition Mechanism is set up and that countries can get the support they need to implement meaningful and just climate action.”
Adam Bandt, the former Greens leader and chief executive of the Australian Conservation Foundation, said countries had “understandably” rejected a pact that he said “failed to even mention the main causes of the climate crisis, let alone address them”.
“The prime minister’s snub of the UN secretary general by failing to mention coal and gas in his speech set the tone early in this summit,” he said.

title: Unemployment to surpass 5% and ‘things will get a bit harder’, treasurer Jim Chalmers warns
text:
Jim Chalmers has warned Australians that “things will get a bit harder before they get easier”, revealing next month’s budget update will show unemployment climbing above 5% alongside slower economic growth for the next two years.
As economists flagged rising recessionary risks, the treasurer used a ministerial statement during question time to reveal what he described as “concerning” economic numbers in the upcoming mid-year economic and fiscal outlook.
Alongside higher unemployment, high fuel costs meant inflation would slow from 4.7% now to only “the mid-3s” by the middle of next year – or about 1 percentage point higher than anticipated in the May budget.
The economy was now expected to grow by less than 2% in both 2027 and 2028.
“We say with humility and with honesty that things might get a bit harder before they get easier,” Chalmers told parliament.
“If Treasury was updating the mid-year forecasts today, they would reflect this difficult environment we’re in. In the near term, they’d forecast softer growth, higher inflation and higher unemployment.”
With a majority of Australians blaming public spending for driving this year’s inflation outbreak, Chalmers promised that the mid-year economic and fiscal outlook will include “net savings” to assist in the ongoing battle against persistently high price pressures.
“It’s not a mini-budget full of new initiatives but it will have some budget-sized savings. At this stage, we expect to more than offset our new spending decisions, without slashing and burning the services people rely on,” he said.
News last week that the unemployment rate had climbed to 4.9% in October has turbocharged fears that a series of Reserve Bank interest rate hikes are weighing more heavily than anticipated – and that the economy could even tip into a deeper downturn next year.
Chalmers said the government’s short-term goal was “cutting spending enough, without threatening growth” – an approach he described as “a delicate balance”.
“We know that no realistic amount of savings makes inflation go away, but too much new spending can make it worse,” he said.
With the full effect of the five rate hikes only likely to become apparent through 2027, Shane Oliver, AMP’s chief economist, predicted economic growth would slump from 2.3%, to below 1%.
“We could flirt with recession next year,” Oliver said, putting the chances of a more severe downturn at a “high and rising” 40%.
Official figures on Wednesday are likely to show inflation climbing to nearly 5%, and Oliver agreed with the treasurer that getting the settings right in the mid-year budget would be “a difficult balancing act”.
“The government has been copping political blame for inflation, and Chalmers is under a lot of pressure to cut [spending]; but if he cuts too much it could accentuate the recession risks.”
The treasurer foreshadowed that any new spending decisions – such as Monday’s announcement that the $25 price cap on prescription medicine would be extended until the end of the decade at a cost of $242m – would be more than offset by savings measures.
But he also flagged that the mix of a weaker economy and “big unavoidable spending commitments” meant bigger deficits in the later years of the forward estimates period.
“It would not be responsible to fully offset these big changes to revenue and payments that flow through automatically from weaker economic parameters,” he argued.

title: Doula thought self-described birth keeper was clinically trained before NSW baby death, inquest hears
text:
A doula who supported a free birth without any medical professionals present has told an inquest that she thought a self-described birth keeper who was assisting her was clinically trained.
The child, known in court as Baby R, died after the free birth. Baby R’s death is one of four being examined in a joint coronial inquest in Lismore, which has heard that three babies died after being born in free births, and a fourth during a home birth between 2022 and 2024.
Sita Tara Kali, a doula who was expected to give evidence later on Monday, was involved in the care of two of the four babies – including Baby R, who is thought to have died of “severe post-maturity” after being born at 43 weeks and one day in a free birth.
On Monday morning, another doula present for Baby R’s birth, Ione Maslin, gave evidence at the inquest.
Maslin told the inquest that she was not medically trained, and had attended about 30 to 40 births before Baby R’s death. She said that Baby R’s birth was the first she had attended without a midwife present.
She told the inquest she now wouldn’t feel comfortable supporting a birth without a midwife present because “doulas need to be working together with the healthcare system”.
The inquest heard that the baby’s mother had hoped that the Byron Bay Birth Centre would be able to provide her with a midwife, but that the she was told she lived too far away.
“She started looking for a private midwife but still she maintained the hope that the hospital would be able to provide her with care,” Maslin, who is from Brazil, told the inquest through a Portuguese translator.
“I insisted for her to go to the birth centre to have the baby … I suggested her to go and visit and feel the energy and to know that it was OK and safe.”
The inquest last week heard that Baby R’s mother had a general distrust of hospitals and felt that having a home birth would give her a stronger connection to her baby.
Maslin told the inquest that Kali had come on as a second doula during the pregnancy. She said she was under the impression that Kali was clinically trained, but was “not a registered professional”.
The inquest last week heard that, at 43 weeks, an ultrasound confirmed that Baby R was extremely compromised. The obstetric advice was urgent, and the mother was urged to attend emergency and strongly advised against a home birth.
The woman contacted Kali, the inquest heard, who said in a police statement that “she was quite upset and anxious. I advised her to go home and rest. ‘Calm yourself down and consider what you want to do’.”
Baby R was born outside into his father’s hands at 9.51am. He was white in colour and never latched on to feed, the inquest heard.
About 14 hours later, the ambulance was called. The umbilical cord and placenta were still attached. Baby R died on the way to a waiting helicopter at 12.22am.
The court heard that Baby R likely died of “severe post-maturity” after being born at 43 weeks and one day. The standard is to induce birth or perform a caesarean section at 42 weeks, as the ageing placenta puts the baby at risk.
The inquest continues.

title: US intelligence chief says he trusts Trump’s description of Putin as ‘my friend’
text:
Jay Clayton, the US director of national intelligence, said he trusts Donald Trump “completely” after the US president called Vladimir Putin “a friend” during their recent meeting in China.
Clayton made the remarks on Sunday, where he was pressed during media appearances on Trump’s warm characterization of the Russian president – who is viewed as a chief US adversary – following his trilateral summit with Putin and China’s Xi Jinping. After a backlash at home and aboard, Trump doubled down on Saturday and posted a photo of himself and Putin shaking hands with the caption “My Friend.”
On CNN’s State of the Union, Dana Bash asked Clayton whether he also thinks Putin is a friend to the US.
“The president is the greatest conductor of foreign policy in a very challenging time that we have seen,” said Clayton on Sunday. “Getting the three nuclear powers together and getting them to agree that they are not going to escalate, that they are going to communicate, that is historic. That is remarkable and, in that context, whatever language the president wants to use, I trust him completely.”
Bash pressed on whether Clayton personally agrees that Putin should be considered a friend.
“Dana, in different contexts, you can use different words. The president pulling off that summit, getting the three of them together, is just remarkable,” Clayton replied.
Speaking with ABC’s Jonathan Karl on This Week, Clayton made similar comments, saying that “using the term ‘friend’ is entirely appropriate” in the context of the summit.
“That conversation, that picture – historic, historic picture – was in the context of the three nuclear powers, the three main nuclear powers, getting together and saying, ‘We cannot have a nuclear incident,’” Clayton said on Sunday, referring to Trump’s post. “In that circle of that conversation, using the term ‘friend’ is entirely appropriate.”
Clayton also dodged when asked again whether he thinks Putin should be considered a friend to the United States.
“Is Vladimir Putin America’s friend? He is not America’s friend in Ukraine. Not at all. Not at all,” Clayton responded.
Last week, Trump sidestepped questions about his views on a friendship with Putin.
“I can’t speak to America,” Trump said in a press briefing. “I have fantastic relationships with Putin, that’s a very good thing.”
Trump’s characterization of Putin has sparked backlash from US lawmakers and officials abroad.
“Who is he? He’s the man who has abducted tens of thousands of children, killed tens of thousands of civilians, targeted civilian infrastructure across Ukraine, detained Americans wrongfully, and continues to do so daily,” Senate minority leader Chuck Schumer posted on social media.
“Embarrassing, despicable, and quite frankly pathetic,” Schumer added. “Senate Democrats will always stand with Ukraine and against Putin and autocratic dictators around the world.”
“It’s beyond me,” Senator Jeanne Shaheen said in an interview with MS NOW. “I don’t understand the president’s admiration and cozying up to Vladimir Putin, who is a war criminal.”
Trump’s comments also drew rebukes abroad, including from the deputy leader of the rightwing party Reform UK.
“It’s just wrong at every level … And it’s a grave mistake,” Richard Tice told Sky News. “He is not our friend, Putin. He is, as others have said, a murderous dictator. And no one is in any doubt about that.”
Trump’s description of Putin as a friend also drew criticism from European allies of Ukraine. “Mr Putin is not our friend and will never be,” the Polish prime minister Donald Tusk said.
Separately, Clayton also faced questions about the recent spate of technology outages across the US and said Americans should expect more disruptions as companies and government agencies replace aging systems.
“And as part of that ongoing upgrade, we are going to have glitches, gaps, interruptions in service,” Clayton said on CNN’s State of the Union program. “That is going to happen.”
- Associated Press contributed reporting

title: Cop31 climate talks break down as key deal rejected
text:
The EU, the UK and allies in the developing world rejected what they called an unacceptable deal on the future of the climate, which failed even to mention fossil fuels, in a dramatic finish to the Cop31 UN talks in Turkey.
The proposed deal “failed to meet the moment”, said Ireland’s environment minister, Darragh O’Brien, speaking for the EU. “We will not endorse a decision that does not respond to the science and that actually risks deepening the chasm between global commitments and the action required. [It] does not even mention fossil fuels.”
As the talks, scheduled to end on Friday, dragged on into Sunday afternoon in the longest climate summit ever, it was clear that the “Antalya pact”, drafted by the Turkish and Australian joint presidencies of the summit, would not achieve the consensus needed to pass.
The Antalya pact invites countries to electrify their economies, calls for rich countries to provide finance to the poor to help them adapt to the impacts of the climate crisis, and calls on countries to minimise the “overshoot” of the 1.5C global heating threshold, of the Paris agreement.
But it failed to endorse the “transition away from fossil fuels” that more than 130 countries demanded, and included controversial provisions on “carbon capture and storage” (CCS) technology that some have said perpetuates fossil fuels.
The presidencies avoided outright collapse of the “conference of the parties” by passing decisions on various related matters, including the “just transition” to help workers in high-carbon industries shift to a low-carbon economy.
But Murat Kurum, Turkey’s Cop president, acknowledged there was no agreement on the draft “cover decision” text and so it had not been adopted.
“We have done our utmost; ultimately, we have not imposed this text on anyone, nor have we issued an ultimatum such as a ‘take it or leave it’ demand,” he said. “It is clear that there are parties in this hall who oppose this text. We recognise that there is no consensus on this document. Therefore, these decisions have not been adopted.”
Many countries, including the EU, UK and developing countries including small island states and some of the poorest countries, said they could not support the Antalya pact deal, which was supposed to be main outcome of the Cop.
In a dramatic intervention, O’Brien said on behalf of the EU that it could not accept the final text in its current form. “It fails to meet the moment … We will not endorse a cover decision or an Antalya pact that does not even mention fossil fuels, which is the key driver of climate change.” He said the EU would not accept a decision “that greenwashes fossil fuels”.
His intervention was met by applause from the hall, and was later followed by similar objections from Panama, the Marshall Islands and Norway.
“This feels like a real line in the sand moment. Countries are standing up to fossil fuel interests and saying no,” said Bill Hare, the chief executive of the advisory group Climate Analytics.
But Mohamed Adow, the director of the thinktank Power Shift Africa, who called it “the worst Cop ever”, said: “The EU has rejected this text, but it cannot wash its hands of the wreckage it helped create ... For countries facing failed harvests, destroyed homes and mounting debt, this amounts to abandonment by the wealthy nations most responsible for the crisis.
“Europe’s hypocrisy is staggering. Its governments demand fossil fuel roadmaps from others while expanding fossil fuels themselves.”
Saudi Arabia defended the decision to include CCS in the text. Other countries, including the Africa group, China and Pakistan, also did not object to the deal, despite some having reservations. Pakistan told the conference that just because a few items in the pact were objectionable to some, the rest should not be sacrificed: “Climate action is not a menu from which we can select only what suits us.”
Ghana also had criticisms of the process but did not reject the final text: “Africa has always chosen to build multilateralism rather than walk away from it.”
Close to 200 countries have been meeting in Antalya for a fortnight under the joint presidencies of Turkey and Australia, with the overrunning talks marked by long periods of deadlock as countries failed to find common ground.
The Cop co-president, Australia’s climate change minister, Chris Bowen, defended his leadership. “Australia left nothing on the field,” he said, but the red lines the presidencies had tried to negotiate were “unbridgeable”.
Asked about the consensus-based system that broke down at the talks, Simon Stiell, the executive secretary of the UN framework convention on climate change, said: “It certainly fell short today,” while emphasising that a significant number of agenda items were passed, with “real progress and concrete results”.
But for many participants, these talks exposed a failure of collective will, particularly of the rich world, to confront the urgency of the climate crisis.
While extreme weather around the world has worsened this year, claiming tens of thousands of lives in heatwaves, in disasters such as the glacier collapse in Nepal, and in droughts and floods worsened by the supercharged El Niño, the slow speed of the climate negotiations appalled even veteran participants.
“There isn’t the sense of urgency to address these issues. That to me is very frustrating,” said Mary Robinson, a former president of Ireland and former UN climate envoy, as the talks neared their scheduled close. “We have co-presidents who haven’t really been stepping up and giving that leadership.”
The UN secretary general, António Guterres, said: “I am deeply disappointed that Cop31 has ended without consensus on an overarching outcome. I share the very profound frustration of all those who expected governments to rise to the moment the climate crisis demands. But this setback does not change the facts. There may be no consensus in the negotiating room. There is no ambiguity in the science.”

title: UK-EU food deal hailed by British firms: ‘We’re pretty aligned anyway’
text:
British producers have broadly welcomed the UK’s deal with the EU, designed to remove the vast majority of physical checks on food, plants and animal products.
The sanitary and phytosanitary (SPS) deal is expected to benefit Britain’s food exporters and will enable UK delicatessens and other small retailers to import European cheese and wine again, something that became economically unviable because of costly Brexit checks.
The agreement is due to take effect on 1 March 2028 and is also intended to reopen the EU market for UK products including fresh sausages, burgers, seed potatoes and molluscs.
However, several years after the UK left the bloc, upending many decades-old trading arrangements, some food exporters said they would remain cautious until the deal came into force.
“Nobody’s going to believe this until it has actually physically happened,” said Iain Barbour, the operations director of the Scottish seed potato producer Jamieson Brothers.
Seed potatoes were not included in the post-Brexit trade deal after the two sides disagreed over certification, halting exports from the UK to the EU despite Scottish seed potatoes’ high health status classification.
The exclusion particularly hit the Scottish industry, whose farmers were among the biggest exporters for the production of chips and crisps in the world, as well as growers in northern England. Scottish seed potato farmers previously accounted for three-quarters of UK production and the sector was worth about £112m a year.
Ireland and the EU represented a fifth of Jamieson Brothers’ trade before Brexit. The company particularly suffered from the loss of the Irish business, given it grew many varieties that were popular on plates in the north and south of Ireland.
While the company adapted its business to start packing work that would have previously been carried out in the EU, Barbour estimates this change cost about £500,000.
“We evolved, we worked with more partners and that’s what kept the business going,” Barbour said.
Barbour is looking forward to supplying his Irish customers once againHowever, he said it would take at least three years until he could revive varieties that were no longer being grown and were instead stored in a seed bank.
“A lot of Scottish farmers stopped producing varieties that were popular in Ireland as they weren’t desired in England. Varieties that had been going about 100 years were killed off in a couple of years,” he said. “So we’ll have to look at bringing them back.”
The planned implementation of the food deal in March 2028 would also be “a couple of months late for the trade”, given most sales happen at the start of the year and the crops needs to be grown in advance.
Barbour anticipates most growers will be wary and will only fully resume trading in 2029. “People are obviously going to be a little bit hesitant to grow anything until it’s 100% official,” he said.
British exporters of live bivalve molluscs – the collective term for shellfish including mussels, oysters, clams, cockles and scallops – hope the deal will give the sector a shot in the arm.
The industry is small and specialised. It was valued at less than £12m a year before Brexit, but it is crucial for some coastal communities.
Offshore Shellfish, a family-run business produces rope-grown mussels in the waters of Lyme Bay, Devon, has managed to continue exporting to its European customers despite the administrative burden and occasional blocks by French customs.
The company exports the vast majority of the blue mussels it produces. It sends to the Netherlands for processing, before most end up in restaurants or on supermarket shelves in Belgium, where they are prized as a key ingredient in moules-frites, one of the country’s national dishes.
Sarah Holmyard, the commercial director of Offshore Shellfish, said the most important detail was an assurance that the deal would allow live bivalve molluscs to be exported even if they did not come from waters with the highest quality rating.
Offshore Shellfish’s farms are in waters which are considered “class A” for most of the year, but before the new SPS deal, any change in water quality to “class B” could have temporarily halted exports.
“That’s a huge win for us because we’ve been pushing and pushing and pushing for that,” Holmyard said.
However, the deal will come too late for those UK shellfish producers that have closed down since Brexit. Three out of four mussel fishing companies in the Menai strait, the channel that separates the north Wales mainland from the island of Anglesey, stopped trading after exports became too difficult.
The promised end of physical border checks on dairy, fish and meat products was welcomed by Rich Clothier, the managing director of Wyke Farms. The Somerset-based cheese and butter maker exports about a quarter of its cheddar to the EU, particularly France, Germany and Spain.
Dairy exports to the EU have been less contentious since Brexit than seed potatoes or mussels, but not without challenges. The removal of veterinary checks is viewed as a significant benefit by Clothier.
“It’s a very bureaucratic process to get everything signed off, in what is not a very modern sort of system,” he said. “The agreement will save a huge amount of cost and product waste as well, because these are perishable.
“Any reduction in friction saves cost, it makes business more efficient. But it is really frustrating that it’s going to take so long [to be implemented] because, to be honest, we’re all pretty aligned anyway.”

title: ‘Serious error of judgment’: outrage over military AI event at Berlin arts complex
text:
With their cavernous post-industrial venues, teeth-grinding four-by-four beats and bouncers that look like Blade Runner extras, Berlin’s nightclubs trade on a reputation for bleakness. A recent event at one of the city’s most legendary clubland institutions, however, has proven too dystopian even for seasoned techno-heads.
On 11 November, the Kraftwerk Berlin arts complex had its central hall transformed into what visitors described as something resembling a war room, with maps and aerial footage projected on to concrete walls, drones hanging from the ceiling, and guards in flak jackets patrolling the premises with sniffer dogs.
Those who flocked to the venue – which hosts the experimental music festival Atonal and is part of the same complex as the techno club Tresor – had come for the launch of Clarity, an AI targeting system developed by the German arms startup Helsing.
Kraftwerk Berlin this week apologised for a “serious error of judgment” and vowed to revise its commercial rental department’s booking policy, after outrage over the event rippled through Berlin’s music scene. The row has raised uncomfortable questions about the commercialisation of the German capital’s famed nightlife, and the culture sector’s traditional pacifism at a time of growing security threats.
The Munich-based Helsing was founded in 2021 and counts the Swedish tech entrepreneur and Spotify co-founder Daniel Ek among its investors and board co-chairs. On its website, it describes Clarity as an agentic intelligence platform designed to use drone, satellite and sensor data to lock on to targets.
It claims that human operators remain responsible for approving any strikes.
Helsing says Clarity is “developed and built in Europe under European control”. The market leader for battlefield software is Palantir’s Maven, the system that has powered US military strikes on Iran this year. European governments have been scrambling for alternatives to US-developed systems. France’s domestic intelligence service has already announced it is dropping Palantir for a homegrown rival.
But European governments’ boosting of their arms industries is also clashing with an anti-militaristic cultural consensus – nowhere more so than in the former cold war pressure cooker of Berlin, where nightclubs became spaces to dance away the anxieties of the arms race.
“The fact there is a war in Europe and that Ukraine needs German support should not mean that we switch off all our critical faculties,” said Michail Stangl, a Berlin-based music curator and DJ. “We are already seeing how AI-driven targeting systems are being used in Gaza, and it’s hard to imagine that once a company like Helsing develops a successful arms system, it would not sell it on to authoritarian regimes, domestic police, or organisations like Frontex to be used against migrants.”
Speaking to the German broadcaster RBB at its launch event, a Helsing spokesperson said none of its military systems were designed to identify persons, and that Clarity was built to seek out objects such as radar systems, launch pads and ships.
It also said Clarity’s agents specialised in “looking for patterns of behaviour”, which could be interpreted as relating to human activity. Helsing did not respond to a request for comment.
The Clarity launch event was condemned in the strongest terms by Tresor, a nightclub and record label that acted as a bridge between post-Wall Berlin and Detroit’s electronic music scene in the 1990s. “It has no place in the spaces our community has built,” it said in a statement.
Tresor’s founder, the Berlin nightlife entrepreneur Dietmar-Maria “Dimitri” Hegemann, is also the managing director of Kraftwerk Berlin. Hegemann has called the booking “unacceptable”, saying it was done by “a staff member at the company responsible for Kraftwerk’s commercial rental business”, without him being consulted. Given his central role at the arts complex, and the level of planning usually required for such a high-security event, this has surprised some Berlin clubland insiders.
That Berlin’s former underground music venues are rented out for commercial purposes is no longer a deviation from the norm. As recently as 19 October, Kraftwerk Berlin hosted an investment summit organised by the German government and featuring a podium discussion between the chancellor, Friedrich Merz, and the chip manufacturer Nvidia’s then chief executive, Jensen Huang.
In a Q&A released after the Clarity row, Kraftwerk Berlin said it had declined a proposed Palantir-sponsored event in 2022 after consulting its cultural teams.
Defenders of such commercial usages point out that many of Berlin’s nightclubs are struggling with rising rents and plummeting bar revenues. Kraftwerk Berlin may not be one of them, however. The total assets of its operating company, Schaltraum Berlin, were reported in June as having a value of €4.3m (£3.6m).

title: Europe is entering a ‘supercycle’ of national elections. Their outcomes could shake the EU’s foundations
text:
In late 1998, Tony Blair was prime minister of Britain, Lionel Jospin was prime minister of France, and Gerhard Schröder had just been elected chancellor of Germany. The EU had 15 member states and pro-European, centre-left parties were in power – either alone or in coalitions – in all but two of them.
Brisk economic growth was lifting living standards. Eastward enlargement was under way. In Washington, Bill Clinton was pursuing the same brand of “third way” centrism as a middle path between free-market capitalism and traditional socialism. The EU felt like it had the tide of history behind it.
Not quite three decades later, the continent’s politics once again seem to be tilting in a single direction – except this time, the momentum belongs to the nationalist far right, and the outcome could be a significant unpicking of the postwar European consensus that built the EU.
Between the end of this month and the end of next year, an extraordinary electoral sequence will sweep the bloc. Voters in four of the EU’s five biggest member states, by population and economy, head to the polls, with parliamentary elections also due in Estonia, Finland, Greece and Slovakia, and regional ballots in Germany.
Spain kicks off the cycle with a snap general election on 29 November, with prime minister Pedro Sánchez’s socialist coalition facing probable defeat to rightwing parties in the shape of the conservative People’s party (PP) and far-right Vox, which already govern together in some Spanish regions.
Next come presidential and parliamentary elections in France in the spring. The clear frontrunner in the presidential race is Marine Le Pen of far-right the National Rally (RN), well ahead of the far-left firebrand Jean-Luc Mélenchon and a hopelessly divided mainstream opposition.
When Poland votes later next year, nationalist parties that between them command nearly half the national vote could well unseat the liberal coalition of prime minister, Donald Tusk, despite recent splits. And in Italy, Giorgia Meloni, whose Brothers of Italy party has far-right roots, hopes to secure a second term in elections due before the end of 2027 – while facing pressure on her right flank from the upstart National Future party.
Paradoxically, this nationalist surge arrives amid strong public support for the EU. Shocked by the chaos of Brexit and seeking reassurance in an increasingly alarming world, a record 74% of Europeans say their country benefits from membership, and very few Eurosceptic parties now advocate leaving outright.
The Eurosceptics and nationalists do, however, still view the bloc as a top-down project that undermines national sovereignty, and aim to transform it into an altogether looser association of sovereign nation-states. In the words of the Italian political scientist Natalie Tocci, that means this coming electoral supercycle could “dramatically change the face of Europe” – triggering not simply “a slow erosion of the European project but a hollowing out, if not an outright implosion”.
All elections differ and national specifics loom large. But analysts agree the underlying forces at work here are connected: sluggish growth, ageing populations, strained public finances and a spiralling cost of living have chipped away at support for Europe’s traditional catch-all centre-left and centre-right parties. The wave of youth-led protests sweeping Europe is only the most visible sign of deep voter discontent.
Meanwhile, nationalist parties have become increasingly adept at conjuring and exploiting an ever-evolving list of supposed threats and crises, from migration and vaccines to the green transition, support for Ukraine, globalisation, international elites and supranational institutions – narratives bolstered by Russian disinformation and overt backing for “patriotic” parties from Donald Trump’s White House. As a result, politics has fragmented, and polarised: nearly one in four voters now backs far-right parties – a share that has grown almost fivefold since the mid-1990s.
The rise has not been linear: over the past year or so, while the far-right Alternative für Deutschland scored a historic regional election victory in eastern Germany, in the Netherlands Geert Wilders’s Freedom party lost nearly a third of its seats, Viktor Orbán’s Fidesz was soundly beaten in Hungary and the far-right Sweden Democrats shed support for the first time in 16 years.
But the underlying upward trend appears clear – fuelled above all, political scientists argue, by the normalisation and mainstreaming of far-right ideas, most notably on immigration. Centre-right parties are gradually dismantling “firewalls” that once barred cooperation with the radical right. At the European level, the centre-right European People’s party has increasingly turned to farther-right groups to roll back parts of the European green deal and tighten migration rules.
For the EU, the biggest impact of this election supercycle could be in the European Council of national leaders, which now features just three centre-left heads of government out of 27. If Eurosceptic leaders in France, Spain and Poland join those of Czechia, Italy, Romania, Slovakia and Slovenia by the end of 2027, they would not have the numbers to rewrite EU law – but they would constitute a formidable blocking minority.
EU budget negotiations, future enlargement, aid to Ukraine and deeper integration in essential fields such as defence, energy, finance and technology could all face paralysis, analysts warn.
Safety in numbers, notes Tocci, could change current leaders’ behaviour in the council. Meloni’s relative restraint has been dictated, in part, by her relative isolation among mainstream peers such as Tusk, Sánchez and France’s Emmanuel Macron (alongside Rome’s reliance on €200bn in EU recovery funds).
If she were instead sitting down with the likes of Le Pen, Poland’s far-right Law and Justice (PiS) leader, Jarosław Kaczyński, and a Vox-backed Spanish government, with National Future’s hardline Roberto Vannacci breathing down her neck at home and those EU funds winding down, she might have less incentive to play pro-EU ball.
Analysts agree, though, that the decisive battleground is France. Le Pen’s election platform sets her on a collision course with Brussels: she aims to cut €11bn from France’s EU budget contribution, hold a constitutional referendum to proclaim the supremacy of French over European law, and breach various single-market rules.
And France “carries very significant influence over the EU”, said Mujtaba Rahman of the Eurasia Group consultancy. Compared with Orbán, he notes, a president Le Pen would have “far more leverage to carry out the far-right playbook of subverting the EU’s law-based, supranational architecture”.
Until now, Brussels has contained disruptors such as Orbán largely because there were rarely more than two or three round the table. A cohesive Eurosceptic bloc would leave the EU unable to enforce rule-of-law standards, further integrate economic and security policies or, indeed, agree on anything much at all. The first victim would very probably be Ukraine, with Le Pen leading a blocking caucus against further aid.
Three decades on from 1998, Europe’s coming elections, concluded Stefan Lehne of the Carnegie Europe thinktank, could well turn into “key tests of the EU’s resilience”. The threat to the bloc might not be immediate or existential, he said, but the medium-term risks were significant.
“A stronger role for the radical right may be unlikely to dismantle the EU as it exists today,” Lehne said, but could “prevent it from becoming what it needs to be to deal with the challenges of the future”. And gradually but inevitably, prolonged failure to act collectively as and where needed would lead a “loss of relevance”.

title: Israel’s destruction of Gaza has created a ‘toxic wasteland’, experts find
text:
Israel’s destruction of Gaza has left a devastating environmental legacy with poisoned water, contaminated soil and toxic air threatening the life-support systems that the population depends on for survival, according to a report.
Israel’s military assault has created widespread contamination across the entire strip, the report by Oxfam and the Conflict and Environment Observatory (Ceobs) finds, with heavy metals, explosive residues, asbestos from destroyed buildings, and sewage making the air, soil and water dangerous for Palestinians for decades to come.
Oxfam International’s executive director, Amitabh Behar, said: “Israel’s ongoing genocide in Gaza includes military assaults on its environment, which are environmental war crimes threatening life now and for generations to come.”
He said the “destruction and contamination of Gaza” have “fundamentally degraded the environmental conditions necessary for human safety and survival” and breach Israel’s legal obligations under international humanitarian and human rights law.
“Palestinians living in Gaza are being exposed to toxins … through air, food, water and via direct contact with contaminated soils and debris. These risks will persist for generations to come, unless clean-up, remediation and recovery actions are prioritised.”
In 2025 and earlier this year, the UN independent international commission of inquiry found that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza and that Israeli officials, including the prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, incited these acts. The Israeli mission in Geneva said Israel rejected the commission’s “libellous sham”. Netanyahu is separately wanted by the international criminal court (ICC) for war crimes.
Oxfam’s report gives the most comprehensive picture to date of what it calls the “toxic wasteland” created by the Israeli assault which has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and wounded at least 175,000, while thousands still remain unaccounted for under the rubble.
Using satellite imagery, remote sensing, scientific analysis and other open-source data, it concludes contamination in Gaza is “widespread, severe and consequential, with serious implications for public health and civilian survival”.
Behar said: “It is horrifying to begin to understand the extent of toxic contamination being faced by the population, who can neither escape nor protect themselves properly from the dangers. In an area as small, oppressed and densely populated as Gaza, continuous exposure is inevitable, with people surrounded by waste and sewage, spreading pests and the risk of disease growing.
“Raw sewage is pouring into the sea and leaking into the ground, while the destruction of Gaza’s sanitation systems leaves people with little protection from the contamination around them.”
He added the “associated health consequences will be severe, with children and pregnant women among those facing the highest risks”.
The UN Environment Programme (UNEP) estimates that Israel’s military operations have generated more than 61m tonnes of debris across the territory, turning Gaza’s destroyed homes, neighbourhoods and infrastructure into a vast reservoir of potentially hazardous materials.
The report’s author, Lama Abdul Samad, a global water and sanitation specialist at Oxfam, said tackling the environmental damage in Gaza will be “highly challenging because contamination is dispersed across the urban rubble, farmland, water systems and soils, while unexploded ordnance continues to restrict safe access to most areas”.
“The analysis highlights the urgent need for Israel to grant access for a detailed environmental assessment on the ground to clarify the risks to public health and identify options for urgent harm-reduction measures. Restoration is likely to require extensive clearance, monitoring and specialised remediation of affected areas from contaminants such as explosive residues, organic pollutants and heavy metals.”
Behar said that as international attention increasingly turned to Gaza’s reconstruction, environmental recovery must not be treated as an afterthought, but as a vital undertaking in parallel.
“Rebuilding Gaza without simultaneously understanding and addressing the extent of environmental contamination risks creating long-term public health consequences for generations to come,” he said.
The Israeli government has been contacted for comment.

title: Netanyahu rival condemns ‘Jewish terrorism’ after settler attacks on Palestinian villages
text:
Arson attacks by militant Israeli settlers on Palestinian villages in the occupied West Bank have caused a political row in Israel, drawing condemnation from Gadi Eisenkot, the opposition leader, who described them as “Jewish terrorism”.
Dozens of settlers raided Palestinian communities overnight on Saturday, setting fire to about a dozen vehicles and several homes and scrawling racist graffiti. At least four communities were attacked. Israeli police said they had launched an investigation with forensic teams.
Photographs from Kafr Malik, near Ramallah, showed one slogan written in Hebrew that read: “This is the first revenge.” Several vehicles and homes had been set alight in the village.
Images from nearby Deir al-Sudan showed vehicles on fire. Palestinian reports said an agricultural building had been set ablaze in Deir Ballut and cars torched in Deir Abu Mashal.
An inconclusive election last month stripped Benjamin Netanyahu, the prime minister, of his majority. Eisenkot has been asked to form a government, though his prospects seem little better.
“Last night’s arson attacks in Judea and Samaria were acts of Jewish terrorism, in every sense of the term,” Eisenkot said, using the biblical name for the West Bank. “Extremist groups that set fire to vehicles and homes are undermining regional stability, putting lives at risk and doing grave damage to Israel’s national security and foreign relations.”
Referring to the far-right ministers Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich, he added: “The actions led by Ben-Gvir and Smotrich in the West Bank have brought the area to the brink of unchecked anarchy.”
Eisenkot, who has been given 28 days to form a government by the president, Isaac Herzog, with a possible 14-day extension, urged the government and security establishment to “use every tool at their disposal – including administrative detention and targeted operations by the Shin Bet – to stop the rioters and impose harsh sanctions on them”.
In an unprecedented rebuke on Sunday, several other members of the Israeli parliament criticised Netanyahu over escalating violence by militant settlers against Palestinians.
Yair Lapid, the leader of Yesh Atid, held Netanyahu’s government responsible for encouraging the attacks. “Jewish terrorism is the product of criminal negligence by the Israeli government,” he said on X, adding that ministers were deliberately encouraging the militant settlers’ violence “through their silence”.
Yair Golan, the leader of the Democrats party, warned of the possibility of a third intifada and described the West Bank as “on the brink of an explosion”.
“Anyone who wants to prevent a third intifada must replace the current government, which provides cover and support for Jewish terrorism and abandons security,” Golan said on X. “Jewish terrorism harms innocent Palestinians and Israeli army soldiers, and pushes Israel toward unprecedented international isolation.”
Noam Tibon, a retired army major general and Knesset member, gave a similar warning. “If Israel does not eliminate Jewish terrorism in the West Bank, it will destroy Israel,” he wrote.
Netanyahu has not yet responded to the accusations.
Australia announced sanctions on Wednesday against three people and four Israeli entities, including a construction company, over their role in the expansion of illegal settlements and human rights abuses against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank.
A day earlier the UK imposed sanctions on eight Israeli construction companies involved in building illegal settlements in the West Bank, which the UN regards as Palestinian territory under Israeli occupation since 1967.
Since the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attacks on Israel, there has been a surge of Israeli settlement expansion and violence against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank. More than 1,100 Palestinians have been killed there by Israeli forces or settlers.
On Tuesday, a 72-year-old Palestinian woman was shot dead in an overnight attack by Israeli militant settlers in a village near Jericho, where the group has recently moved in after taking over several Palestinian homes.
Reuters contributed to this report

title: Briton swims length of strait of Hormuz to highlight environmental cost of war
text:
A British endurance swimmer has completed a three-day swim through the strait of Hormuz to highlight the environmental cost of the Iran war.
Lewis Pugh, a UN patron of the oceans, swam the 9.3-mile (15km) length of the waterway, which is a key route for oil shipments from the Middle East.
According to the Lewis Pugh Foundation, he witnessed several attacks on commercial shipping, explosions in the distance and fighter jets overhead.
An oil tanker was struck by a projectile about 2.5 miles from where he was swimming on the first day. On the second, he saw flames rising above a headland separating him from a burning liquefied petroleum gas carrier, Tara Gas, and later he passed close to the vessel while it was still on fire.
“My immediate thoughts were for the seafarers onboard,” Pugh said. “The flames were enormous. These vessels carry highly flammable gases, and an attack on one can have catastrophic consequences, not just for crew members but also on the surrounding marine environment.”
The 56-year-old undertook his first swim in a conflict zone to urge an end to the fighting, the reopening of the strait and action to address environmental damage caused by the conflict.
Believed to be the first person to attempt a long-distance swim in the strait since the conflict began in March, Pugh swam a route from Musandam Island, carving through the dramatic mountains and inlets of Oman’s Musandam peninsula and Iran’s spectacular mangrove forests, to reach the Cape of Hormuz at the peninsula’s northern tip.
He said: “War causes immense human suffering. Lives are lost, families are torn apart and homes, hospitals and schools can be destroyed in minutes. But there is another casualty that receives far too little attention: nature itself. And the damage can last long after the fighting has stopped.”
The small expedition team included a support boat and kayak that remained alongside Pugh during the swim.
Pugh said environmental damage caused by conflict often received less attention than the human cost. According to the UN, at least 175 vessels have been attacked since fighting began, and about 30 attacks have caused significant pollution.
The strait of Hormuz is one of the world’s most important shipping routes and is also home to wildlife including dugongs, sea turtles and whale sharks.
Pugh, who was born in Plymouth, said oil spills and other contamination could have long-term consequences for marine ecosystems including coral reefs, seagrass meadows and mangrove forests.

title: Iraq university’s removal of male professors teaching women sparks weeks of protests
text:
The removal of male professors teaching female students at a university in southern Iraq has sparked protests and been criticised by activists as a Taliban-like gender segregation policy.
As many as 400 women are estimated to have joined protests over the past two weeks calling for the return of their professors at Al-Qadisiyah University in a move that appears to have surprised its administrators.
The university said the move was necessary to “prevent the mixing” of men and women and had been requested by the families of female students. But students said their families had known since before they enrolled that there were men on the teaching staff and supported their daughters’ protest.
Students said university bosses had mocked their protests and refused to discuss their concerns about the sudden loss of their academic supervisors. On social media, commentators also accused the women of seeking to keep male professors to “establish immoral relationships with them”.
“My classmates and I went to demonstrate, and the university president, Rahi al-Yasiri, blocked our path with his bodyguards, who then began making fun of us. He ordered them to take photographs of our faces, in an attempt to intimidate us and punish us later,” said Huda, 22, one of the female students.
Huda said the students tried to explain how men and women still worked together in society in Iraq. “Aren’t there doctors who treat both men and women? Why then do you prevent male professors from teaching us, too?” In response, Huda said Al-Yasiri replied: “Even if you hit your heads against the wall, I will not bring back the professors.”
The students said a large number of them were tied to graduation projects and research supervised by the professors. They said they had grown accustomed to their professors’ teaching methods, who also knew their students’ strengths and weaknesses, which made replacing them at this stage more complicated.
Female students said they had been told by the university that if they were not happy with the change, they should drop out.
An Iraqi-British feminist researcher, Balsam Mustafa, from the University of Cardiff, said the female students were “treated as if they are minors without the right to object to decisions affecting their academic lives”.
Mustafa said the removal of the male professors was a part of a worrying trend in women’s rights in the country, with “growing discussion about women’s clothing and chastity reflected in the celebration of female students who wear the abaya”.
An Iraqi lawyer and human rights activist, Israa Salman, said the restrictions on women was a “societal catastrophe”.
“Attempts are being made to suppress women’s talents and turn Iraqi society – a society that has produced remarkable minds and expertise, with women playing pioneering roles in many fields – into something resembling Kabul under Taliban rule.
“This contradicts Iraq’s constitution and the international treaties and conventions the country has signed and ratified,” said Salman.
Produced in collaboration with Jummar, an independent Iraqi media platform

title: Myanmar ruling gives new relevance to genocide convention and is ‘full of messages’ for Israel
text:
The international court of justice (ICJ) verdict making Myanmar the first country in history to be found guilty of committing genocide does not just deliver justice for Rohingya victims. It also gives the 1948 genocide convention new relevance in governing the actions of nation states.
In their nine votes to six majority ruling, the panel of judges in The Hague set out a detailed roadmap for how the convention should be applied to real-world situations in which a government is accused of committing genocide against a whole population group, especially when it comes to assessing the question of intent.
The lengthy judgment will have been read particularly carefully by Israel, the only other country currently before the ICJ accused of genocide.
It is also relevant to Germany, which has been brought before the court by Nicaragua on the accusation it has facilitated and failed to prevent genocide in Gaza.
“I think it’s a judgment that brings the genocide convention alive,” said Philippe Sands, a leading human rights lawyer who was part of the Gambian legal team. “It gives the convention practical, real meaning. And if the alternative view had been taken, the convention would essentially become a dead letter.”
Amnesty International’s secretary general, Agnès Callamard, called the ruling “a rare moment of justice for survivors, victims and their families”. But it was also an assertion of humanitarian law in an increasingly lawless world.
“This is a good day for international law. We needed it,” said Dr Iva Vukušić, an assistant professor in international History at Utrecht University and a war crimes expert. “It is really important, clarifying a lot of law, and that’s going to be very helpful going forward.”
There will be a spillover from this ruling to its sister tribunal in The Hague, the international criminal court (ICC), providing a benchmark for when genocide charges could be made against individual perpetrators.
The Trump administration, instinctively hostile to international legal institutions, is also watching critically. The US ambassador to the UN told the ICJ before this judgment not to “lower the legal threshold for proving genocide” lest it be “weaponised” against US and allied soldiers.
The court did not directly lower the standard for demonstrating genocide, and the Gambia – which brought the case to The Hague – did not ask it to.
The judges kept the existing benchmark for judging genocide intent as the “only reasonable inference” of Myanmar’s actions and referred extensively to prior case law. But it went a long way towards clarifying how that standard should be applied in assessing atrocity crimes committed by states.
Before this case, only Serbia had faced the charge of genocide at the ICJ, in cases brought by Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. In the Bosnian ruling in 2007, Belgrade was found to have failed to prevent the 1995 genocide in Srebrenica, but in both cases it was cleared of committing the genocide directly.
The new ICJ judgment finds the Myanmar military directly responsible for genocide against the Rohingya, a Muslim minority targeted in a ferocious counterinsurgency campaign that reached its peak in 2017.
In assessing the Myanmar campaign, the ICJ looked not just at the death toll of about 10,000 in assessing the scale of the atrocities, but at the total Rohingya population targeted in northern Rakhine state, 815,000 people. Significantly, it cast its net wider than just the death toll, considering mental damage done to the survivors, particularly victims of sexual violence, and the impact on reproduction in the Rohingya community.
Most importantly, the ICJ judgment provided a guide to interpreting the standard set by Serbian cases, in which a finding of genocide could be made only if there were not other plausible motives for mass killing.
In this judgment, the court ruled that Myanmar could have had other motives, such as the desire to displace or punish the Rohingya population, but that those motives could exist alongside genocidal intent. The judges said genocidal intent was the “only reasonable inference” from the “totality” of evidence.
In justifying that conclusion the judges pointed to several factors that international law experts say are relevant to the Gaza case, which is now hearing written pleadings and is expected to take at least another three years.
The common factors include the targeting of children, which the court described as striking at the “foundation” of the Rohingya as a group – the ICJ said up to 2,109 Rohingya children under the age of five had been killed, while more than 5,000 Palestinian children under five years old have been killed in the Gaza war.
Another incriminating factor cited by the court was the “bulldozing and large-scale terrain clearance” after the destruction of villages, followed by “rapid construction” including security installations, which has been the hallmark of Israeli army occupation of over 60% of the Gaza Strip.
“It’s full of messages for Israel,” said William Schabas, an international law professor and expert on genocide at Middlesex University. “There are obvious differences, of course, the evidence will be different, but if you exchanged the word Myanmar with Israel, you wouldn’t have to change much in the judgment.”
The fact that there were six dissenting voices on the bench suggested that substantial parts of the majority’s reasoning were not beyond dispute, and lawyers involved in the case cautioned that it did not necessarily mean that the same bench would find Israel guilty of genocide in Gaza. But the same lawyers added that the opposite was almost certainly true. If this case had failed, the case brought by South Africa against Israel would have been all but over.

title: Indian opposition party’s youth wing warns of more Meta protests after police clashes
text:
The youth wing of India’s main opposition Congress party warned of more protests against Meta’s removal of some of its members’ accounts, a day after clashing with police outside the tech firm’s locals offices.
In Hyderabad on Friday, protesters carrying placards and chanted slogans as they stormed into the building that houses Meta’s offices, smashing plants to the ground and clashing with police, according to footage released by the Indian Youth Congress’s X account.
The Indian Youth Congress on Saturday posted warnings on X that it would “storm your offices across the country and stage protests” unless the Instagram accounts of its leaders were restored.
Two such accounts were restored after Friday’s protests, but thousands of accounts of journalists, creators and influencers critical of the government remain restricted, Manu Jain, who is in charge of social media for the youth group, told Reuters on Saturday. Meta must explain how its algorithms restrict posts and must restore accounts taken down on government orders, he added.
India is Meta’s biggest market by users and the company declined to comment on Friday’s demonstrations.
Debate is growing in India about potential risks to free speech from the increasingly strict efforts of Narendra Modi’s government to remove social media content it objects to. India’s IT ministry did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Meta has said it restricts content in India to comply with local laws.
Modi’s government says it orders content to be taken down only if it breaches local laws, can harm public safety or national security. Congress has long accused Meta and other social media platforms of curbing dissent online by removing accounts.
A video from Friday’s demonstration showed protesters spray-painting anti-Meta slogans on walls outside the building that houses its Mumbai office and clashing with security guards who tried to stop them.
In Gurugram near New Delhi, Congress workers chanted slogans and held banners reading “restore youth Congress accounts”, online posts showed.
An opposition politician from Telangana state criticised Congress workers over what he called vandalism at Meta’s Hyderabad office, saying it had undermined the city’s reputation as a safe destination for businesses.
Pradeep Bhandari, a national spokesperson for Modi’s ruling party, also criticised Congress’ actions on Saturday, saying they had “not only vandalised and destroyed Meta’s office in Hyderabad” but were also “flaunting it on social media”.
“This is Congress Model: Vandalise offices of Private companies,” he wrote.
Reporters Without Borders has said the removal of journalistic content from social media has been on the rise in India this year, and free speech activists say a new government rule gives social media companies hardly any time to review and decide on takedown requests.
In February, Modi’s government ordered social media companies to take down unlawful content within three hours of being notified about it, tightening an earlier 36-hour timeline.
Meta disclosures show that it restricted more than 5.4m posts or accounts in India under local laws in the first half of 2026, second only to Indonesia and up from about 70,000 in the whole of 2025.
“The large majority of these items included instances where we were obligated to proactively restrict content … based on local law requirements,” Meta said.

title: When you see smoke, run: Rohingya who escaped Myanmar’s genocide tell their stories
text:
Smoke was often the signal to run – seen from a distance, it was the indication for Rohingya that a neighbouring village was under attack and that theirs would be next.
In other places, they saw the rivers run red and would pull out the bodies, perform quick burial rites and then flee.
What happened during the escape from Myanmar – a journey through forests and over hills and rivers while being battered by monsoon rains – was a key part of the ruling made this week in The Hague that Myanmar had carried out a genocide against the Rohingya.
The international court of justice (ICJ) said it was not enough to say they had faced ethnic cleansing when soldiers had also killed those trying to escape – Myanmar was trying to destroy the group as a people.
Stories of that violence in 2017, of organised mass killing, sexual attacks and the complete destruction of their villages, came with the refugees who arrived in neighbouring Bangladesh, eventually numbering more than 700,000 and settling in what has become the world’s largest refugee camp.
For months, they would arrive from places such as Tula Toli, where thousands were rounded up, killed and buried in mass graves. In other villages, men were captured and killed by the security forces.
Many survivors had escaped an attack on their own village, only to watch their relatives being killed in the villages where they had sought safety.
Almost a decade later, the majority of Rohingya who arrived in 2017 remain in the refugee camps, joining those who had already been there since the early 1990s, having escaped previous military operations and ever-increasing persecution.
The ICJ ruling has come at a particularly harsh time for Rohingya refugees, in a year in which hundreds have died at sea trying to escape the refugee camps, and in which countries such as Malaysia and India have spoken about returning the Rohingya to Myanmar.
Rohingya campaigners are hoping that this ruling will put an end to that.
Rohingya refugees still live in fragile shelters made of bamboo and tarpaulin sheets. They are denied the right to leave the camps, to work or to seek education.
Below are some of the stories from Rohingya who arrived in Bangladesh in 2017, having escaped Tula Toli and the surrounding area.
Momtaz and Dildar Begum
Sitting in the background, almost unnoticed as Momtaz Begum recollected how Myanmar forces had killed her husband and children and then raped her in front of her lone surviving child, was a woman who seemed to know every word of the story.
It was not because she had heard it before. Dildar Begum had experienced exactly the same violence as her sister had, in their village, Tula Toli.
In fact, they had for months believed each other dead until they discovered that they had both made it to Bangladesh and lived in different parts of the camp.
Each had only one surviving daughter, both of whom had similar scars along the back of their heads.
Anwara Begum
Twice previously Anwara Begum had lived as a refugee in Bangladesh. Once as a child in 1978 and then again in the early 1990s, as a young mother who lost her son to a respiratory disease during a rainy season spent in a flimsy tent.
When she was forced to return to Myanmar, though the persecution she fled there had not stopped, Anwara swore to herself that she would never become a refugee again.
She broke that oath when she saw the river by her village filled with bodies floating from Tula Toli.
Her husband first pulled from the river as many bodies as he could to bury and then they gathered some belongings and headed westwards to the River Naf – the border with Bangladesh.
To cross, she handed over all the gold she owned, equal to US $200 (£150), to a Bangladeshi boatman.
Nur Alam
Elderly people were not spared the Myanmar military’s attacks. Like so many others, Nur Alam had to be carried on the shoulders of his children on his journey to Bangladesh.
His 10-year-old grandson, Mamoon, held his hand. Once in the camp, they stuck to each other.
Alam’s arrival in Bangladesh was his fourth time being a refugee there. He was first expelled from Myanmar – known as Burma until 1989 – during military operations in the 1950s when Bangladesh was not yet an independent country.

title: Indian man sentenced to 19 years in prison for conspiring to kill Sikh separatist in New York
text:
An Indian man was sentenced to more than 19 years in US prison on Friday after admitting to orchestrating a failed Indian government-backed plot to kill a Sikh separatist in New York City, in connection with what US and Canadian authorities have called a broader effort to target Indian dissidents.
Nikhil Gupta, 55, pleaded guilty in February to murder-for-hire, conspiracy to commit murder-for-hire and conspiracy to commit money laundering.
The US district judge Victor Marrero handed down the 235-month sentence at a hearing in a Manhattan federal court.
The discovery of alleged assassination plots against Sikh separatists in the US and Canada has tested relations with India, which has denied involvement in such plots.
Prosecutors accused Gupta of plotting with an Indian government official to kill Gurpatwant Singh Pannun, a dual US-Canadian citizen and lawyer at Sikhs for Justice in New York who has advocated for a sovereign Sikh state in northern India.
Gupta and the Indian government official, Vikash Yadav, arranged to have $15,000 in cash delivered to a purported hitman who was actually an undercover US law enforcement officer, court papers show.
Yadav is also charged in the case but is not in US custody. It is unclear whether he has hired a defense lawyer.
India’s government has dissociated itself from any plot against Pannun, saying it was against government policy.
Prosecutors with the Manhattan US attorney’s office had recommended a sentence of about 24 years in prison.
“This case cuts to the very core of American values,” prosecutor Ashley Nicolas said in court. “We don’t condone the use of violence to silence voices in this country, ever.”
Addressing the court on Friday, Gupta said he regretted straying from the non-violent example set by the Indian independence leader Mahatma Gandhi.
“I’m sorry to Mr Pannun, I’m sorry to the communities I hurt, I’m sorry to my own family,” Gupta said.
Pannun told the court that he was grateful to the US for prosecuting Gupta and said he would keep advocating for Sikh sovereignty.
“Self-determination for my people and my homeland, Punjab, is my lifetime goal,” he said.

title: US reacts cautiously to Myanmar genocide ruling as EU praises ‘critical’ role of UN’s top court
text:
The US has greeted with caution the world’s highest court’s ruling that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority, while China has raised concerns of judicial overreach.
Reactions to Thursday’s historic ruling underlined deep international division over the role of the court and similar institutions. The international court of justice (ICJ) had never previously found a state responsible for genocide and the decision could set a precedent for future genocide claims, notably a case against Israel.
The EU hailed a “landmark” judgment from the ICJ, while the UK reaffirmed “full support” for the court and the international legal order. Australia called on Myanmar to comply fully with the judgment and its obligations under international law.
But China, which has offered rare international support for Myanmar’s military rulers since they seized power five years ago, highlighted “issues such as jurisdiction overreach and expanded interpretation”.
“China … believes that such practices are not conducive to the settlement of disputes,” the foreign ministry spokesperson, Guo Jiakun, told a news briefing when asked about the ICJ ruling. “The international community should make joint efforts in this direction to avoid complicating this issue.”
Western nations cut ties with the unstable and poor south-east Asian country after the 2021 coup that ousted a civilian-led government.
Myanmar’s presidential spokesperson said on Friday that the ruling was “unfair”, noting the judges’ nine to six vote. The country’s military rulers have denied carrying out a genocide, claiming their actions targeted a Rohingya militant group that conducted insurgent attacks.
“When we look at the result, not all 15 judges agreed with the decision,” said Khaing Khaing Soe, speaking at a press conference in the capital, Naypyidaw. “So this was not a unanimous decision … I would say it is not fair.”
The US state department said on Thursday that Washington was examining the judgment, while stressing the need to avoid “politicisation” of the ICJ.
Donald Trump’s administration has taken a dim view of international law, vowing to dismantle the international criminal court (ICC), but has yet to question the legitimacy of the ICJ.
The state department reiterated US support for the people of Myanmar and said it shared “grave concerns over the continued abuses of human rights against Rohingya Muslims and members of other minority groups”, noting that the US was the largest single humanitarian donor to the Rohingya humanitarian crisis response.
In Brussels, the EU said Myanmar must fully implement the ICJ’s ruling “without delay” and that “compliance with ICJ’s decisions is not optional, it is an obligation under international law”.
“The European Union holds the ICJ in the highest regard and remains steadfast in its support for its critical role in the peaceful resolution of disputes and the upholding of the rule of law at international level,” an EU spokesperson said in a statement.
“The Rohingya people have endured immense suffering, including displacement and violence, and their plight must not be forgotten. This landmark ruling underscores the imperative of justice for victims and the necessity of upholding international law.”
The UN secretary general, António Guterres, called the ruling “a demonstration of international justice and a reaffirmation that impunity for such horrific acts must not stand”.
The UK expelled Myanmar’s defence attache and called for measures to “ensure the court’s ruling sends a clear message that such crimes cannot be committed with impunity”.
The ruling caps a lengthy legal campaign since August 2017 when Myanmar’s military launched what it called a “clearance campaign” in Rakhine state in response to an attack by a Rohingya insurgent group. Reports rapidly emerged of mass rapes and killings by security forces, as well as the burning of thousands of homes.
Judges rejected Myanmar’s claim that its actions were primarily intended as counter-terrorism operations, or even that they were an attempt to punish or forcibly displace the population but without committing genocide.
The country’s leader, Min Aung Hlaing, who headed the military during the 2016-17 attacks, has a pending arrest warrant from the ICC – which, unlike the ICJ, prosecutes individuals and not states – on allegations of crimes against humanity.
The former general overthrew the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi, triggering a civil war that has left tens of thousands dead. He was installed as civilian president in April after elections that were widely discredited.
While the ICJ does not have the power to enforce rulings, its decisions are considered binding, carry diplomatic weight and can shape international action, including sanctions.
Under the 1948 convention, to establish that genocide occurred the court had to find that there was an intent to destroy the Rohingya “in whole or in part”.
About 1.2 million Rohingya refugees now live in Bangladesh, primarily in crowded camps across the Cox’s Bazar district, where they endure harsh conditions marked by fire hazards, infectious diseases, monsoon landslides, inadequate sanitation and strict work restrictions.
Judges at the court based in The Hague have also been asked to rule on other allegations of genocide.
South Africa has accused Israel of breaching the genocide convention during its offensive in Gaza, a claim Israel vehemently denies. That case is years from completion. An interim ICJ judgment in 2024 ordered Israel to ensure its forces do not commit acts of genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.
Ukraine also has a case pending against Russia. Shortly after Moscow’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, Kyiv accused Russia of fabricating genocide claims against Ukraine to justify the attack.
