title: ‘Everyone struggled for this justice’: tears in court as Rohingya vindicated in Myanmar genocide ruling
text:
There were tears in the halls of The Hague in the Netherlands and an eruption of applause in the refugee camps of Bangladesh as the scattered communities of Rohingya watched the UN’s top court rule the Myanmar military had committed genocide against them.
For almost a decade, the Rohingya have awaited this moment; recognition from the international court of justice (ICJ) that Myanmar in 2017 intentionally tried to destroy the mostly Muslim minority group through a campaign of mass killings and rape. More than 10,000 Rohingya were killed and 700,000 fled to neighbouring Bangladesh.
By the time they spilled into the court’s halls, the relief was evident. A Rohingya community leader threw a big thumbs up as he left the courtroom and others immediately took out their phones to call family in the refugee camps.
Salma, 30, a Rohingya survivor who lost family members in the 2017 genocide, said: “Everyone worked hard and struggled for this justice, for this cause. When they hear it today, everyone will be happy, thank God. I don’t know how to express it or even what to do with myself.”
Another Rohingya present, who cannot be named because of safety concerns, said they cried as the judge went through each of the rulings.
“During the last few minutes I couldn’t even sit down any more, I had to move to the back because I didn’t know how I’d react,” they said. “I saw some of the other Rohingya around me crying. They were so emotional.
“Now the responsibility is with the international governments. It has been declared genocide now and they have to act.”
In Bangladesh, where most of the Rohingya population have lived – in the world’s largest refugee camp – since being forced to flee in 2017, the verdict was translated into the Rohingya language for the crowds who had gathered to watch on screens specially set up for the purpose.
They immediately leapt up, cheering, applauding and shouting gratitude for the Gambia – the faraway African nation that brought the case to the ICJ on behalf of the stateless minority. Many held posters that read “Thank You Gambia” and “Justice = Safe Return”.
“Since we arrived here, we have been waiting and looking forward to this justice,” said Farida Khatun, 50, who has been a refugee in Bangladesh since 2017, when her village, Tula Toli, was targeted by soldiers. The village in north-western Myanmar, near the Bangladesh border, was the scene of a massacre in August of that year, with reports of mass killings and gang rapes.
She said, however, that she does not expect to be able to return home. Tula Toli was completely destroyed by Myanmar’s forces and no longer exists. “Even though today’s verdict makes us happy, my heart still cannot believe that they will take us back in true peace.”
The case has taken seven years to reach this point, with Rohingya researchers working to collect testimony from survivors. The initial hope for justice had faded during the long wait for a ruling. Many were also left deflated during early hearings when the one-time pro-democracy hero Aung San Suu Kyi defended the Myanmar military at The Hague.
Before today’s ruling, some were optimistic, others were prepared to be disappointed, but all said they knew themselves that they were victims of genocide.
The tension was finally released when the court declared Myanmar was responsible for genocide against the Rohingya, highlighting the use of sexual violence and attacks on children alongside the killing of Rohingya who tried to flee violence, which it said meant the violence amounted to more than ethnic cleansing.
The court ordered Myanmar to provide reparations for the Rohingya and end continuing breaches of the genocide convention.
There is now also an international criminal court investigation into the violence of 2017, looking specifically at the crime of mass deportation, and for which prosecutors in 2024 sought an arrest warrant for Myanmar’s leader, Min Aung Hlaing.
With continuing violence against the Rohingya, the possibility of a return to Myanmar, as happened after previous exoduses to Bangladesh in 1978 and the early 1990s, remains unlikely.
But many hope the ICJ ruling will be the start of a process of ensuring justice and lead to real international pressure to ensure their safety in Myanmar.
“We will be able to return to our homeland – with our rights, with our citizenship, and having received our full security. We will be able to return,” says Salma.

title: Fewer than half in UK will pay TV licence fee within a decade, report warns
text:
Fewer than half of households in Britain will pay the BBC’s licence within a decade, according to analysis that warns that the broadcaster’s funding is locked in a “spiral of decline”.
With senior BBC figures concerned about the accelerating fall in licence fee sales, the independent projections also warn that the proportion of households paying the levy will further decline to less than a third by 2037-38 should the government persist with the corporation’s current funding model.
Lisa Nandy, the culture secretary, is preparing to publish proposed changes to the licence fee that will force anyone who watches a streaming service to pay it. Currently, only people who watch live TV or the BBC’s iPlayer have to pay the fee.
Projections by the respected independent media consultancy Oliver & Ohlbaum Associates point to an “unsustainable” cycle of falling income leading to lower spending on strong content that attracts audiences.
They show the BBC’s licence fee income – paid by 77% of households last year – could be worth less than half its current level in real terms by 2037-38, the next point at which the broadcaster’s funding model is renegotiated.
The BBC’s own internal licence fee income modelling is also said to be bleak, with the corporation already making painful cuts to programmes and staff.
Nandy’s proposed new funding model, which could form part of the BBC’s next 10-year charter, is expected to be published before the end of the year.
Extending the licence fee to streamers would put the BBC on a more sustainable footing. However, it will be controversial with major streamers such as Netflix, Disney, Amazon and YouTube, as well as their subscribers.
Other more radical proposals, such as a household levy for the BBC, have already been ruled out by the Treasury as politically impossible.
Like all media companies, the BBC is facing a myriad of pressures. The costs of making television have hugely increased, while the arrival of streamers and digital platforms has transformed viewing habits.
Meanwhile, freezes to the licence fee over the past decade, as well as extra costs loaded on to the BBC by previous governments, have given the corporation less to spend.
The new independent projections, included in a report on the BBC by the Reset Tech thinktank, show why the broadcaster’s leadership and ministers accept that the status quo cannot continue.
The study suggests the BBC’s spending on TV content will more than halve by the next charter review. BBC viewing per person via TV sets would fall from 46 minutes a day in 2024-25 to just 23 minutes a day in 2037-38. Revenue would fall from £3.8bn to £1.6bn in real terms.
The BBC remains the UK’s most-used media brand, reaching 94% of adults every month. However, the projections suggest YouTube could overtake BBC TV set viewing in 2032-33.
It is predicted that more than half of households will not pay the licence fee by 2033-34. Non-payment of the licence fee has already risen from about 9% of households in 2015 to about 23% last year, and the trend has been accelerating.
Dylan Sparks, the UK director at Reset Tech, said the report confirmed that the BBC’s current funding model was broken. “The BBC is critical national infrastructure and it deserves a long-term settlement that ensures it not only survives but thrives in the decades to come,” he said.
“We urge the government to defend this vital British asset and to use the BBC charter renewal process to come forward with a new funding model that is universal, affordable and sustainable.”
A BBC spokesperson said: “We have consistently argued that the current funding model is not sustainable and needs reform. We will continue to engage with government to secure a new charter that provides sufficient, sustainable and universal funding so the BBC can deliver for audiences for generations to come.”

title: Manchester’s Co-op Live arena evacuated after apparent tear gas incident at Don Toliver concert
text:
Police have evacuated Manchester’s Co-op Live arena after a substance believed to be teargas was let off in the crowd during a Don Toliver concert.
Greater Manchester police said the incident occurred near the end of the US rapper’s show on Sunday evening.
Greater Manchester police said concertgoers had been safely evacuated, with several people being assessed on site for side effects as a precaution and inquiries under way to determine what the substance was. No serious injuries have been reported.
Assistant chief constable Steph Parker said in a statement: “Our priority was to ensure the safety of every person that was attending the concert.
“Several people were treated on site, and one has been taken to hospital at this time. Anyone who has left the event and since become unwell is advised to attend their local hospital.
“We understand the concern that this incident will have raised – particularly those with loved ones at the venue last night – and we’d like to thank everyone for their patience as we dealt with it.
“There were over 12,000 people in attendance during this concert who were safely escorted from the arena so they could make their way home.”
She continued: “Our declaration of a major incident has allowed us to ensure emergency services and partner agencies can work together quickly and effectively to coordinate a safe response.
“We will now begin to fully understand what this substance was and how this incident came about.”
The north-west ambulance service said one person was taken to hospital and more than 50 were assessed by clinicians.
The service said in a statement: “We deployed several emergency crews, including our Hazardous Area Response Team, to support the safe assessment and treatment of people at the scene.
“More than 50 people have been assessed by our clinicians, with some reporting eye and respiratory symptoms. Decontamination is being carried out as a precaution and one patient has been taken to Manchester Royal Infirmary for further assessment.
“The incident remains ongoing and our teams remain at the scene assessing and caring for patients. We continue to work closely with emergency service partners while inquiries are carried out to establish what the substance was.
“Anyone at tonight’s event who has since noticed side effects or become ill should seek medical advice.”
Footage shared on social media appeared to show concertgoers coughing and covering their mouths as they left the venue.
Co-op Live has the capacity to hold 23,500 people, with American singer Phoebe Bridgers scheduled to perform at the venue on Thursday.
Don Toliver is partway through the UK leg of his Octane World Tour.

title: Theresa May’s blast from the past calls Tories back to their unhappy place | Peter Walker
text:
Anyone who accidentally switched to BBC One at about 9.45am on Sunday to be greeted by Theresa May awkwardly espousing the virtues of Brexit could have been forgiven for thinking they had woken up in around 2018 – and not being especially pleased at the idea.
This is one of the problems now facing May’s party. For all that it is a reflex action for Conservatives to push back against closer ties with the EU, Andy Burnham’s decision to pursue such a course plunges them back into their own unhappy place.
For Tory MPs and activists with a full set of Brexit campaign medals, this risks being especially triggering. May’s repeated attempts to cobble together a departure deal that could unite her party involved repeated humiliations, among them the heaviest ever parliamentary defeat for a British PM, when the Commons rejected her Brexit plan by a majority of 230.
With the afterglow of Boris Johnson’s “get Brexit done” 2019 election triumph now seven years and four prime ministers ago, under Kemi Badenoch the party has opted to do less of the, in David Cameron’s resonant phrase, “banging on about Europe” and instead focus on policy areas such as the economy, social security and defence.
In a speech to the CBI conference on Monday, Badenoch will condemn Burnham’s new deal with the EU, sealed at last week’s Brussels summit, but based on the argument that he botched the negotiations, not that closer links as such are bad in themselves.
“If we can make our trading relationship better, good. I’m all for working on a smarter deal,” she was to tell the business leaders’ gathering.
The reasons for this caution are obvious. To begin with, even more ardent Tory Brexiters struggle to articulate any tangible benefits to the UK in the decade since the referendum, beyond slightly niche constitutional points about self-determination.
In her BBC interview, May, who comments sparingly on live political subjects despite being an active Tory peer, did not even try to argue that Brexit had been a success, instead saying it was impossible to know, given events such as Covid and Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, and then adding: “I don’t think Britain’s state today is about whether or not we left the European Union.”
Many voters are much clearer about what they think. Polling suggests that a clear majority of Britons view Brexit as both a failure and a mistake in the first place, with similar support for rejoining the EU, although this depends in part on the pre-conditions for doing so.
This is a product of both lived experience and what pollsters delicately call “demographic churn” – that is, the death of many of the disproportionately older Britons who voted leave and their replacement on the electoral rolls by younger people with more positive views about the EU.
A new constituency-level poll on Brexit sentiment found that hundreds of previously leave-backing areas, including Burnham’s Makerfield seat, now support rejoining.
Of the 632 Commons seats in England, Scotland and Wales, it found that voters in 512 would rejoin the EU, with 47 too close to call. Just 73 areas – slightly over 11% of the total – still want to stay out.
For the Conservatives, the battle has not ended. Badenoch will lambast the PM when he sets out his new EU deal in parliament on Monday. Her deputy, Alex Burghart, has already promised that a future Tory government would unpick it.
But make no mistake, Europe is no longer the Conservatives’ defining political thread, and division, as it was for several decades. May might, understandably, be unable to move on from the issue that made her PM and then destroyed her career. But her party, like the country, has no choice.

title: NHS savings drive leaves hospitals in England facing ‘unpalatable’ cuts
text:
Dozens of hospitals are so short of money they may not be able to continue caring for patients and are being forced to make “unpalatable” cuts to services and staff, the Guardian can reveal.
Thirty-one health service trusts in England have issued stark warnings that NHS demands for them to make huge budget savings this year threaten their ability to function normally. All have declared that as a threat in the register of risks they have to maintain and publish.
Twenty-seven of those trusts are in such dire financial straits that they have rated lack of money as the biggest threat they face. Six have given that danger a rating of 25 – the highest possible score – in their risk register. A much-larger number of trusts have launched cost-cutting programmes to save as much as £106m each this year by limiting the services they provide and shrinking their workforces, despite understaffing being widespread across the NHS.
The six include King’s College hospital NHS trust in London, which is seeking to save £85m this year, and the St George’s, Epsom and St Helier hospital group, also in the capital, which has a savings target of £91m. The others are the North Midlands, Gloucestershire, and Doncaster and Bassetlaw acute trusts, and Birmingham and Solihull mental health trust.
Trust bosses say their finances are in a “precarious” and “severe” state. They blame rising drug prices, strikes and the cost of covering pay rises, the extra demand caused by this summer’s heatwaves, and the introduction of electronic health records. Privately they accuse NHS England of forcing them to adopt unreasonable savings targets in order to help the health service as a whole balance its books, because hospitals have been told to stop overspending.
In an illustration of the impact that savings drives can have, in August people in Kent with cancer had to wait up to a month for appointments before they could start chemotherapy; this was because the cancer unit had fewer nurses on duty than usual after the East Kent trust cut rates of pay to work extra “bank” shifts as part of a cost-cutting plan, which led to understaffing.
The trust admitted in a paper, which its board discussed, that it was seeing “increasing waits for new patient appointments and pre-chemo appointments … due to lack of take-up of bank shifts due to [pay] rate changes”.
In September, York and Scarborough trust said it would shut a 28-bed ward at Bridlington community hospital, a “step-down” facility that looks after people recently discharged from hospital before they go home, to help it save £1m. It did so despite the risk this will add to pressures on beds at its two acute hospitals.
The trust also looked into withdrawing the maternity and radiology services it provided at Whitby community hospital as another of its “opportunities for efficiencies”, to save an estimated £200,000. However, those plans were “no longer being considered”, it said. It is also considering cutting the opening hours of the three urgent treatment centres it runs in York, Scarborough and Malton, to save a further £200,000, even though such services are intended to prevent overcrowding of A&E units. The trust refused to answer questions the Guardian asked about that.
Harrogate and district trust has decided to stop providing out-of-hours GP care in Hambleton and Richmond, covering a large swathe of rural North Yorkshire, after 15 years because it can no longer afford to do so. It is unclear who will offer patients that service in the future.
Sherwood Forest trust’s plan to close a hydrotherapy pool at King’s Mill hospital in Sutton-in-Ashfield, to save £150,000 to £200,000, has provoked an outcry. The pool is used to help rehabilitate about 1,500 patients a year, including those with long-term health conditions or those recovering from car crashes or a hip replacement, said the local Labour MP, Steve Yemm.
Sara Hazzard, of the Chartered Society of Physiotherapy, said: “The proposed closing of this pool is deeply concerning and risks depriving vulnerable patients of vital specialist rehabilitation. For people with chronic long-term conditions, aquatic physiotherapy is a clinical lifeline. The warmth and buoyancy of the water help people to manage pain, exercise and maintain mobility when land-based rehabilitation may not be suitable.”
Sherwood Forest also recently admitted in a paper discussed by its board that “financial restraints, including the need to reduce bank and agency spend, may lead to impacts on ability to maintain patient care and safety”.
Torbay and South Devon trust is axing 199 non-clinical posts and charging staff more for parking and food to help it meet its £54.4m “cost improvement plan” target. It has an underlying deficit of £100m.
In a paper submitted to its 5 November board meeting, it said it would “assess all available options to close the forecast risk gap and deliver financial plan, including ‘unpalatable’ and high-risk options”. NHS England has told its leaders to break even this year or risk having their performance being reviewed, which could lead to them being replaced.
The NHS is so short of cash that it cannot afford to have the number of beds it needs to help hospitals cope this winter, Emma Rowland, NHS England’s executive director for performance and recovery, told MPs earlier this month.
One trust boss said: “I have been a [trust] chief executive for more than 10 years and the NHS’s finances are as tough as they have ever been. Many trusts are forecasting deficits larger than recent years. Balancing the books often means breakeven. Very few trusts will break even and many will miss their financial plan for this year.”
Trusts are also cutting jobs in a desperate effort to save money. For example, Nottingham university hospitals trust plans to shrink its workforce by 1,279 to help it meet its £106m savings target for 2026-27. It admits that a third of its identified savings are “high risk”.
Similarly, Barts health trust in London aims to axe 1,100 posts to save money.
Dr Tony O’Sullivan, a co-chair of the campaign group Keep Our NHS Public, said: “This financial straitjacket on the NHS is deeply irresponsible and the consequences are devastating. Years of underinvestment have left trusts being asked to make huge savings while demand and costs keep rising.
“AI can’t staff a ward, and another reorganisation won’t reopen a single bed. Closing step-down beds means some patients will spend longer in hospital waiting for somewhere safe to go. That leaves fewer beds for people waiting in A&E and makes it harder to carry out planned operations.”
O’Sullivan added that Yvette Cooper, the health secretary, should ask the chancellor for emergency funding for the NHS to help it cope with the pressure it is under. The Department of Health and Social Care’s total spending for 2025-26 was £217bn, most of which went to the NHS.
NHS England did not respond directly to a request for comment over the widespread cost-cutting. A spokesperson said: “The NHS did an amazing job last year to bring its finances in within budget for the first time in more than a decade, while also delivering record levels of treatments and operations to patients.
“This has been another challenging year, and NHS boards are rightly being transparent about financial risks and taking action to mitigate them. Across the NHS, organisations are working hard to improve productivity, live within their means and make the best use of taxpayers’ money, while continuing to deliver the care people need.”

title: Russell Brand’s wife vows to abide by prison rules after video controversy
text:
Russell Brand’s wife, Laura, has promised to “absolutely honour” rules set by the prison where her convicted sex offender husband is being held, in another YouTube video published on Sunday.
This week Andy Burnham called on Google to take down a video uploaded to Russell Brand’s YouTube channel last Sunday that contained a statement from the disgraced comedian in prison, where he is serving a 10-and-a-half-year sentence for rape and sexual assaults.
Laura Brand began the latest episode of Sunday Service – described as a Christian series, which the couple started together six months ago – by telling viewers: “Last week’s episode drew considerable amount of attention and now that I understand the parameters set by the brilliant and professional staff at HMP Littlehey, I will absolutely honour that.”
She went on to address scrutiny regarding her continuing to run her husband’s YouTube channel, amid a Ministry of Justice inquiry focusing on whether Brand has broken rules that are supposed to prevent “serious distress” to the victims of crime.
“I am choosing to continue Sunday Service because I really enjoy it,” she said. “It is also a place where I will continue to be proud to be a wife, a mother and a woman defending her family at a time when the media’s image of what kind of a woman I am is under so much scrutiny.”
In the previous episode, the first published since Brand was jailed – after being convicted of one count of rape and three sexual assaults at Southwark crown court on 5 November – Laura Brand read out a message from him protesting that he was not guilty.
The video, titled “The Good Work Continues”, has remained on YouTube despite ministers repeatedly asking for it to be removed.
That video has now accumulated more than 1m views, becoming the best-performing video on Brand’s channel since 18 May, when he interviewed the New Testament scholar Jeremiah Johnston. Prior to that, the last time Brand surpassed 1m views was on 5 December last year, when he published a video conversation he had with the American conservative influencer Candace Owens. Many of his videos in the past year have drawn only between 50,000 and 100,000 views.
On Thursday night, Burnham said he “wouldn’t leap” to changing the law to force social media companies to take down such content. But he added: “I would call on those social media companies to take these interviews down. You know, why are we having to hear from him? We shouldn’t be, and certainly [the victims] shouldn’t be hearing from him.”

title: Video of ICE detaining father and daughter while boarding flight sparks protests in Seattle
text:
Protesters marched through the Seattle-Tacoma international airport on Sunday after widely shared footage captured masked immigration agents detaining a father and daughter on an airport jet bridge as they boarded their Alaska Airlines flight.
Video of the incident on Saturday – filmed by fellow passengers – quickly went viral on social media, sparking condemnation from lawmakers, including Washington Democratic governor Bob Ferguson and Seattle mayor Katie Wilson.
Footage and photographs showed protesters with bullhorns and signs that read “ICE out of Washington” and “Abolish ICE” at the Seattle airport. Protesters could be seen walking inside and around the airport chanting “ICE out now” and other rallying cries.
“I made my view very clear to Alaska Airlines: They need to call on ICE to get out of our airports,” Ferguson said in a briefing. “I’ll be making that request of every other airline that operates at SeaTac airport as well.”
On Sunday a lawyer representing Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza and his daughter, Sofia Hernandez Mejia, said they were heading to a family baptism ceremony in California when they were detained by masked agents.
Other passengers boarding the Alaska Airlines flight at Seattle-Tacoma international airport used their cellphones to film the father and daughter being detained by the officers, who were wearing unmarked jackets and khaki pants.
The videos show the officers struggling with someone on the ground. The flight, bound for Los Angeles, was delayed.
ICE has stepped up operations at airports since the summer as the agency has shifted tactics from sweeping urban raids to more targeted operations in all corners of US, with arrests reaching record levels.
Ferguson called ICE’s tactics “deeply un-American” and called for the agency’s abolition.
“The video is horrific and it is chilling,” Ferguson said at a news conference on Saturday with labor leaders and local elected officials.
Wilson called ICE’s tactics “unacceptable and un-American”.
In a statement to the Guardian, ICE said its officers detained Mendoza, an immigrant from Mexico, who it said had overstayed his visa “in violation of our nation’s laws”.
According to the ICE statement, Mejia “hurled hot coffee on the officers”. ICE said she was in the US illegally from Mexico and had overstayed her visa. She could be charged with assaulting a federal officer.
The father and daughter were travelling to attend a baptism and were seeking asylum in the US, where they had lived since 2015, their lawyer, Olia Catala, told the Associated Press. They had no criminal record, Catala said.
Mejia, who is in her mid-20s, had married a US citizen and filed paperwork for adjustment of her status, the attorney said. Mejia’s husband – who was not detained -was accompanying Mejia and her father when they were detained on Saturday, Catala added.
“They’ve done everything correctly, and these are educated people,” Catala said of the father and daughter. “She went to college, to university, she worked for a nonprofit. No criminal history [for] any of them. So it’s just heartbreaking.”
Both were being held at the Northwest ICE Processing Center in Tacoma, Catala said.
She said Mejia was carrying a cup of coffee when the confrontation occurred. “When somebody’s charging at you, you’re going to drop a cup of coffee,” Catala said.
“It was just a lot of commotion, and honestly, if somebody is running at you or charging at you and they’re not wearing a uniform, you don’t know who they are,” Catala said. “There was a lot of panic, chaos, not knowing what’s going on.”
Alaska Airlines said ICE officers gave no advance notice of the enforcement action, which occurred during a busy travel weekend ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday. The airline said it was working with the Port of Seattle, which manages the airport, to see if protocols were followed, and had raised concerns “directly with the appropriate authorities”.
The Port of Seattle said in a statement that the arrest was distressing not only for the family but for other passengers, and that local authorities would “engage federal officials to understand more about what occurred”.
The Associated Press contributed reporting

title: US army to blow up bomb-making chemicals despite safety concerns
text:
The US army plans to invoke emergency provisions to avoid a court order that had put on hold plans to detonate several tons of bomb-making chemicals in Iowa, saying that continued delays will make it more dangerous as the weather starts to turn colder.
“To protect its personnel and the surrounding communities, the Army needs to take swift action,” government lawyers told the eight US circuit court of appeals in a filing late on Saturday. “Protection of human health and the environment demand action now, not delay.”
The army plans to detonate the chemicals by Tuesday.
Environmental groups criticized the government’s move, decrying it as a maneuver to get around a court order and avoid public demands for safety and transparency.
The appeals court on Thursday granted a request by environmentalists to put on hold a permit that cleared the way for the detonation in Middletown, a small community about 160 miles (257km) south-east of Des Moines. It was initially planned for Friday, but the army later announced that it would push the operation to Monday after an outpouring of public concern about potential health and environmental effects.
Environmentalists have called for a review of the emergency permit that was approved earlier this month by the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA).
In a statement on Sunday, the Iowa Environmental Council, Sierra Club and Earthjustice questioned claims that all alternatives were given appropriate consideration.
“The Army seemed more concerned over the weekend with finding a way to sidestep the judicial process than on meeting the public’s demands for greater transparency, notice to affected communities, and far stronger protection of people, property, and the environment from serious harm,” said Thien Chau, an attorney at Earthjustice.
Government lawyers said the army doesn’t need a permit to take emergency action against an immediate threat from explosive material.
They said the standards of a federal law regulating hazardous waste don’t apply in situations when there is an immediate threat to health, safety or the environment as determined by an explosive or munitions emergency response specialist.
Officials contend that the chemicals are unstable, and the risk of an uncontrolled explosion is growing, particularly as temperatures drop. They said there is a risk that the chemicals may explode as temperatures are expected to drop below 30F (-1C) in the coming days.
In March, staff at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant found several dozen barrels of degraded lead azide, which is used in munitions production. Crystallization of the material created an unstable and dangerous situation, prompting the army to assemble experts in munitions chemistry, engineering and environmental safety to come up with a plan.
According to EPA documents, alternatives such as neutralizing and decomposing the drums’ contents with other chemicals were considered. But officials said handling the drums would increase the probability of an accidental, fatal detonation.
The environmental groups disagreed, arguing in their petition that other alternatives were not fully considered. They also criticized officials for not sharing more information with the public.
Nearly 400 people live in Middletown, but thousands more in surrounding areas could be affected by detonated material that could disperse in the air and land on the ground.
Iowans in the region were told to stay inside, keep windows and doors closed, bring pets and livestock indoors, and clean cars, windowsills and outdoor surfaces after.
“The detonation will result in an air plume with some lead-containing particles which will disperse in the air and deposit on the ground,” an advisory states. “Lead is toxic to humans and animals.”

title: Trump hosts third crypto gala for meme coin amid conflict of interest outcry
text:
Donald Trump is scheduled to headline his third cryptocurrency gala on Sunday night at his country club in Virginia, rewarding top holders of his own meme coin as Democrats accuse the president of improperly profiting from his crypto ventures.
The dinner, set to take place at the Trump National Golf Club in Sterling, Virginia, will include meet-and-greets with Trump supporters including the boxing champion Floyd Mayweather, Shark Tank investor Kevin O’Leary, NBA champion Tristan Thompson and mentalist Lior Suchard, according to the event’s website.
The gala’s access and perks are divided by tiers for the 185 holders of $TRUMP, the president’s meme coin. A Trump fragrance, a poster, a “commemorative” ticket, and a “Trump watch” are reserved for 120 attendees. Meanwhile, the top 29 investors are invited to a VIP reception, and the top four will receive a “TRUMP 18K Gold Watch”.
Trump has hosted two similar galas since he took office last year, bringing a flurry of criticism as Democrats accuse Trump and his family of monetizing his brand through an array of equities and crypto ventures while in office.
After sweepingwins in the midterms, Democrats have vowed to investigate conflicts of interest involving Trump and his personal wealth during his presidency. They also say they plan to push for legislation that would ban activities such as the meme coin gala dinner.
“This dinner and scoring mechanism appear carefully constructed to increase investment in $TRUMP, allowing the President to abuse the power of his office to personally enrich himself, as he has throughout this term,” reads a letter sent by Adam Schiff and eight other US senators last month.
Since returning to the White House, Trump has made more than $1bn from his crypto businesses, according to financial disclosures released in June. Trump received more than $500m from his World Liberty Financial business selling new crypto products, and raked another $600m from sales of souvenir-type “meme” coins stamped with Trump’s face. Trump launched his $Trump meme coin days before his inauguration.
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Interest in the $TRUMP coin dinner has plummeted, with contestants’ combined holdings dropping from $148m in May 2025 to $8.6m in this month’s gala.
More than half of the digital wallets publicly listed on the contest leaderboard for Sunday’s dinner are tied directly to crypto exchanges that bar US-based users, indicating they are linked to foreign nationals, according to an analysis of blockchain data prepared for Reuters by the nonpartisan, non-profit consumer advocacy group Public Citizen.
“Neither the President nor his family has ever engaged — or will ever engage — in conflicts of interest,” White House spokesperson Anna Kelly told Reuters earlier this year. “President Trump proudly made the United States the crypto capital of the world through executive actions.“
The Trump family’s other crypto-connected equities and ventures have also fallen in value to record lows. Together, outside investors in their five main crypto and crypto-linked projects have lost more than $5bn, according to a Reuters analysis.
The Trump meme coin has earned the Trump family at least $635m, according to the president’s June financial disclosure statement. In total, the Trumps had earned at least $2.3bn through April from their four main crypto ventures, including the meme coin.
The president’s stake in a fifth crypto-linked venture, Trump Media & Technology Group, is worth about $430m.
Reuters contributed reporting

title: Abdul El-Sayed doubles down on ‘TrumpCare’ health plan, urging president to ‘get it done’
text:
Michigan US senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed on Sunday doubled down on naming healthcare reform legislation after Donald Trump as long as it meant the president would not impede its passage.
“If he’s open to the conversation, I am open to it, too,” El-Sayed said of Trump on Sunday. “If the president is opening to signing that bill, let’s get it done.”
El-Sayed made those remarks on Sunday on NBC’s Meet the Press, where he reiterated his pledge to pursue a single-payer, national healthcare program after the Democrat became the first Muslim person elected to the US Senate during the midterms earlier in November.
Trump’s Republican party is going to lose control of Congress for the second half of his second presidency. But the president has made clear his intention to wield his legislative veto powers whenever he sees fit.
Appearing on Sunday’s Meet the Press, El-Sayed said he would not mind Medicare for All – a big part of his campaign platform – being named “TrumpCare” as long as such a program came into existence.
“I care that the people of this country finally have the unmet promise of guaranteed healthcare in this country. And if the president is serious about leaving a lasting legacy, there is nothing better than the ultimate Trump card,” El-Sayed said to Meet the Press host Kristen Welker, making a double entendre for a term that – when the T is lowercase – also refers to a card that beats out others in card games.
El-Sayed told Welker that such a Trump card would be in effect “from the moment [people] are born to the moment that they pass away – that guarantees them the healthcare that has been so elusive in this country without premiums, co-pays and deductibles”.
The senator-elect’s comments come after he previously suggested to CNN that he is not above stroking Trump’s prodigious ego to get legislation passed – including by naming Medicare for All “TrumpCare”.
He also previously wrote on social media, alongside images of a gold health insurance card with “TrumpCare” inscribed on it: “Donald, this is on the table. Guarantee healthcare for every American, from cradle to grave.”
Trump seemingly responded to El-Sayed’s post by reposting a screenshot of the senator-elect’s tweet. Trump has not formally responded to the push to create universal healthcare.
Trump has spent much of his second presidency trying to get as much as possible named after him – from institutions, physical buildings and currency.
El-Sayed also said that he supports healthcare reform proposed by Bernie Sanders, the progressive US senator.
Sanders’ proposal would create a single-payer system in which the federal government insures everybody, financed by an increase in taxes, while eliminating private insurance.
But El-Sayed said he is not focused on eliminating private insurance as an option, which Sanders aims to eliminate by having everything primary and preventive services to hospital stays covered under his proposed plan. Out-of-pocket costs on deductibles and co-pays – staples of the rapacious private insurance industry to which most Americans must resort – would also be eliminated under Sanders’ plan.
El-Sayed said he wants to “provide you basic public health insurance no matter who you are in this country” while being open to the idea of not taking alternative options away.
The senator-elect said he has a meeting on the books with JD Vance. El-Sayed would not share the agenda of the meeting, but he confirmed that the vice-president’s chief of staff contacted him after his election victory.

title: Jensen Huang’s reported affair was ‘most expensive sex since Helen of Troy’, US senator says
text:
Invoking Greek mythology, US senator John Kennedy has characterized former Nvidia chief executive officer Jensen Huang’s reported affair with a suspected Chinese spy as “the most expensive sex since Helen of Troy”.
The Louisiana Republican’s allusion to the legendary figure whose desirability was such that it caused the mythic Trojan war came during an interview on NBC’s Meet the Press on Sunday. Host Kristen Welker asked Kennedy, known for his colloquialisms, if US national security was put at risk by Huang’s affair, given the position his company’s chips have occupied at the forefront of the artificial intelligence boom.
Huang stepped down as Nvidia’s CEO on 12 November after allegations surfaced of extramarital relationships with the suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang and two Nvidia employees.
Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, had been executive director of Megaspeed International. Megaspeed facilitated about $12bn in chip sales, in violation of export controls in the US, where the Trump administration has prohibited the selling of advanced AI chips to China.
On Sunday’s edition of CNN’s State of the Union, the Trump administration’s national intelligence director, Jay Clayton, said he suspected China was able to obtain Nvidia’s most advanced AI chips.
He also said on Fox News Sunday: “There are chips that have ended up in places that they should not.”
Kennedy said he was “less interested in … what [Huang] did” than in asking the Trump administration’s commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick, and its treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, about how China was evidently able to circumvent US “export controls”.
“Mr Huang … did what he did. I hope he had a good time. It was the most expensive sex since Helen of Troy,” Kennedy said.
Lutnick has faced scrutiny over allegedly ignoring warnings that Megaspeed was smuggling chips to China. Other administration leaders, including Bessent, wanted to put Megaspeed on a trade blacklist – but the commerce department stalled enforcement of it.
Kennedy said he could only conclude commerce department leaders are either “so incompetent you wouldn’t put them in charge of a food truck” – or “they knowingly allowed this to happen”.
He said he wanted to get Bessent and Lutnick under oath in front of a Senate committee to “answer some hard questions”.
“And if secretary Lutnick is giving our chips away, he needs to stop it, in my opinion,” Kennedy said.
Bessent said on Sunday’s edition of CBS News’s Face the Nation that the Trump administration had been in touch with Nvidia’s temporary management, lead directors and lawyers while trying to find out who was in charge of compliance at the company.
“It behooves Nvidia to move quickly on this because we want to know what the culture was,” Bessent said on the program.
Kennedy, a former Louisiana state treasurer who began his political career as a Democrat before switching parties and becoming a staunch Trump administration ally, delivers many of the colloquialisms that have become his calling card with a southern US drawl.
Many believe Kennedy resorts to the drawl to come off as folksy – while he holds degrees from Vanderbilt University, the University of Virginia School of Law and the UK’s Oxford University, and is estimated to be one of the wealthiest US senators.

title: Belgium’s airports set to shut down due to anti-austerity strike
text:
Belgium’s airports set to shut down due to anti-austerity strike
Skeyes halts air traffic control services, grounding flights at Belgian airports amid union-led strike.
Nearly all flights are set to be cancelled in Belgium on Monday after the country’s air traffic controller said its staff would take part in a national strike against government austerity measures.
Skeyes, the company responsible for Belgium’s air traffic control, said it would be unable to provide regular services at the country’s airports and in its airspace between 7am (06:00 GMT) and 9pm (20:00 GMT) on Monday.
“The anticipated staffing levels will not allow the safe handling of regular air traffic to be guaranteed during this period,” the company said. “Skeyes is therefore obliged to temporarily suspend the services concerned.”
It added that only essential services for emergencies and other safety-critical flights would continue.
The Brussels-Charleroi airport, a major European hub for low-cost airline Ryanair, said the strike would result in the “complete shutdown of all the country’s airports for an entire day”, affecting thousands of passengers.
“Without air traffic control, no flights can take off or land,” the Brussels-Charleroi airport said, criticising a “last-minute decision” with “disastrous consequences”.
Brussels airport said most departing and arriving flights “will have to be cancelled”.
Pushback against austerity policies
Belgian unions have called for a nationwide day of action on Monday to protest against austerity and reform measures pursued by the country’s governing coalition.
The Board of Airline Representatives in Belgium, which represents about 25 carriers, said the walkout would be the 11th strike affecting Belgian airspace in 11 months.
The unions also plan a large-scale demonstration in Brussels on Monday. Significant disruption is expected to public transport, while schools, government offices and refuse collection services may also be affected.
Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever has been in protracted talks with his coalition partners on a cost-cutting budget that will save 10 billion euros ($11bn) over the next few years by Monday, in a bid to reduce the country’s high deficit.
Earlier in November, De Wever offered his resignation after his coalition failed to reach a deal. However, Belgium’s King Philippe rejected the resignation and gave the prime minister more time to find a solution.

title: Indonesian police remove 24 body bags from factory fire site
text:
Indonesian police remove 24 body bags from factory fire site
Authorities in Java are searching for dozens of missing workers as they continue to battle remaining hotspots.
Indonesian authorities are set to resume the search for missing workers on Monday after police removed 24 body bags from a factory in Java gutted by a fire.
Firefighters continued to battle remaining hotspots on Sunday after the blaze broke out on Saturday evening at the PT Fonusa Agung Mulia candy factory in Cikande, Serang regency, West Java province.
A search for dozens of missing workers was suspended overnight but would resume Monday morning, Hendra Kurniawan, the police chief of Indonesia’s Banten province, told local broadcaster Metro TV on Sunday.
Steven Erwin Wijaya, the CEO of the factory’s parent company, PT United Family Food, said at a news conference that about 300 people were present for Saturday’s shift, with 65 of them believed to have been in the affected area when the fire broke out.
In a statement that followed, the factory said 24 of the 65 workers had returned home, four were receiving medical treatment, 29 remained missing, and the whereabouts of another eight had yet to be confirmed.
At a news conference on Sunday, Wahyu Hidayati Dwi Palupi, a police disaster victim identification official, said the intensity of the fire had made it impossible to identify the recovered victims visually. She said they would collect DNA samples from relatives and the personal belongings of the missing workers, a process that could take two to three weeks.
The number of dead was not immediately clear. Police said that one body bag could contain parts of more than one person.
Authorities said the cause of the fire was being investigated. Parts of the building remained at risk of collapse, an official added.
Photos and videos circulating online on Sunday showed flames and thick smoke coming from the factory, which borders the capital, Jakarta. Footage from inside the three-storey building appeared to show the fire caused extensive damage, with equipment blackened and destroyed.
Indonesia has suffered several deadly fires in recent years.
A fire in an office building in Jakarta killed at least 22 people last December. An explosion at an Indonesian nickel-processing plant killed at least 13 people in 2023.

title: US intelligence chief defends Trump’s comments calling Putin his ‘friend’
text:
US intelligence chief defends Trump’s comments calling Putin his ‘friend’
US Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton says Trump’s comments were ‘entirely appropriate’ in the context of the summit.
United States Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton has faced pressure to justify President Donald Trump’s claims that his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin is a “friend”.
In an appearance on the ABC News show This Week, journalist Jonathan Karl pressed Clayton on Trump’s recent remarks.
“Is Vladimir Putin America’s friend? Because Trump said he couldn’t answer that question,” Karl asked.
Clayton responded by calling Trump’s meeting “historic” and his remarks “appropriate”, but the intelligence chief also clarified that the US has not taken Russia’s side when it comes to the country’s invasion of Ukraine.
“Is Vladimir Putin America’s friend? He is not America’s friend in Ukraine. Not at all. Not at all,” Clayton said.
The scrutiny follows a first-ever confirmed meeting between Trump, Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping on November 19.
The three world leaders had a roundtable on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) conference in Shenzhen, China.
Throughout his presidency, Trump has repeatedly praised Putin. In August 2025, Trump hosted the Russian leader in Alaska for Putin’s first visit to the US in nearly a decade.
Upon reuniting with Putin at the Shenzhen conference, Trump offered him a warm, light-hearted greeting.
“Who is he?” Trump joked, first pointing to Putin, then striding across the room to shake his hand. “He’s my friend.”
Trump has since doubled down on his remarks, posting several images of their meeting on social media, one of which bore the caption, “My Friend”.
When a reporter asked whether Russia was a “friend to America” in a news briefing on Friday, Trump brushed aside the question.
“I can’t speak to America,” Trump said, proceeding to explain that he and Putin had grown close during an investigation into whether Russia had interfered in his favour during the 2016 US presidential election.
“I’ve been dealing with Putin during the fake Russia, Russia, Russia hoax. And to be honest, he was very nice about it,” Trump explained.
The US State Department has long been critical of Russia over allegations of human rights abuses, including the torture and imprisonment of political dissidents.
Washington has also supported Ukraine after Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, providing billions in security assistance and weaponry.
Under Trump, however, that support has cooled, with the US president openly criticising his Ukrainian counterpart, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, for failing to cut a deal with Russia.
Such remarks have divided Republicans, with critics like outgoing US Representative Don Bacon accusing Trump of “playing footsie” with Putin.
“Traditionally, Republicans stood up to Russia and China,” Bacon said last week. “We stood for freedom, and we stood up for countries that shared our values. President Trump has been terrible on this, right here.”
But in his television appearances on Sunday, Clayton defended Trump’s remarks, describing the president’s statements of friendship as “entirely appropriate” for building a personal rapport with the Russian leader.
He also praised Trump for uniting some of the world’s biggest powers for a conversation about nuclear proliferation.
“It should be assuring that you have the three world nuclear powers getting together and saying: We’re not going to go in that direction,” Clayton told This Week.
While the trilateral meeting concluded with a statement about “reducing nuclear risks”, critics point out no firm commitments were made.
Also on Sunday, in an appearance on CNN, Clayton reiterated his support for Trump’s remarks.
“In that context, whatever language the president wants to use, I trust him completely,” Clayton said.

title: ‘Extremely concerning’: Inside a US Army plan to detonate Iowa lead stores
text:
‘Extremely concerning’: Inside a US Army plan to detonate Iowa lead stores
The US Army plans to invoke emergency powers to detonate 4 tonnes of lead azide in an Iowa town, despite a court-ordered stay.
The United States Army intends to detonate more than 4 tonnes of lead azide at a military base in Iowa, defying a federal appeals court’s order suspending its permit to do so.
In a fact sheet this weekend, the Iowa Department of Health and Human Services said that two controlled explosions were scheduled for around noon (06:00 GMT) on Monday.
That announcement follows statements from the Department of Justice, arguing that Tuesday was the cut-off date to carry out a planned detonation.
Lead azide is a key explosive used in military ammunition. The Iowa stockpile has reportedly grown unstable, and Justice Department lawyers have warned that sub-freezing temperatures could trigger an uncontrolled explosion.
“The real choice, in other words, is not between a detonation and no detonation. It is between a planned and mitigated detonation and an unplanned and unmitigated explosion,” their court filing said.
But critics have questioned the army’s rationale for pushing ahead with the planned detonation, despite the court order to pause it.
“Anyone can claim an emergency at any point and do whatever they want. I don’t think people can or should accept that,” said Thien Chau, a lawyer with the legal group Earthjustice, which represents the plaintiffs in the lawsuit.
Chau told Al Jazeera that not enough has been done to mitigate the risk from the explosions, which are expected to release a cloud of lead into the air.
Experts say there is no safe level of lead exposure, and the dense metal can cause birth defects, brain damage and infertility.
“Anyone who hears that the army plans to explode nearly 10,000 pounds [4,500kg] of [this chemical] would recognise that that is not normal,” Chau said.
“That is extraordinary, and that is not something that you just take lightly.”
An 11th-hour legal battle
The impending explosions come after a tense legal battle between the US government and environmental groups, including the Sierra Club and the Iowa Environmental Council.
The groups have questioned the legality of an emergency permit the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) granted on November 13. The EPA authorised the Army to move forward with the explosions, originally scheduled for November 20.
The plaintiffs pointed out that nearby residents were only given a week’s notice and that the blasts could send lead dust as far as 160km (100 miles).
They also argued that the EPA failed to properly assess safer disposal methods.
The US Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit granted a pause on Friday. But in a Saturday court filing, the Justice Department maintained that the Army could still proceed with the two controlled blasts under an emergency exemption.
“The emergency exception does not depend on the Emergency Permit and is therefore not affected by, nor contradictory to, the terms of this Court’s administrative stay,” the Justice Department said in its filing.
But Earthjustice has argued that such a manoeuvre would sidestep the court’s authority.
Government lawyers have “laid the groundwork for a possible detonation without a permit, which would effectively bypass judicial process and review”, lawyer Rachel Rintelmann wrote in a Friday filing.
A crisis ‘of the Army’s own making’
The controversy centres on a deteriorating stockpile of explosives stored for more than two decades at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant near the city of Middletown.
The stockpile contains roughly 9,700 pounds (4.4 tonnes) of lead azide across 68 barrels, with lead accounting for approximately 6,900 pounds (about 3.1 tonnes) of its chemical mass.
The explosives had been kept in a mixture of water and ethanol to ensure their stability. But in March, military technicians at the facility discovered that the system was breaking down.
According to a court declaration, an Army munitions expert found that the liquid in the drums had evaporated, causing needle-shaped crystals to form.
That recrystallisation puts the lead azide at risk of exploding on its own, as a result of temperature charges or even friction. So many crystals had formed that it was no longer safe to even open the barrels, according to the expert.
But on Sunday, Earthjustice released a statement questioning how this problem was allowed to develop in the first place.
“This emergency is of the Army’s own making,” the statement said. “The Army has not publicly provided details about why the lead azide was not disposed of before it became so dangerous. ”
The US Army has said the barrels are set to be detonated in place at the Iowa facility.
But it claims to have explored other options as well. According to the Army’s environmental assessment, it has previously considered two alternatives: chemically neutralising the explosives, or transporting them to an on-site detonation facility.
It rejected both ideas due to concerns that handling or transporting the explosives could trigger an accidental detonation.
Burying the drums, meanwhile, risked subjecting the shock-sensitive material to jolts that could similarly cause an unintended explosion.
What should residents do before and after the explosions?
But the health risks of even a planned explosion have put residents and environmental groups on edge.
On November 15, the Army released two plume maps outlining the potential spread of lead contamination across a swath of eastern Iowa, though projections hinge on real-time wind conditions.
The first map traces what could happen if a lead-bearing plume drifts northward, with a potential airborne trajectory over communities like Burlington, Muscatine, Davenport, Iowa City and Cedar Rapids.
The second map presents a more tenacious problem: surface exposure.
As the plume tracks north, heavier lead-bearing particles are expected to coat the landscape, landing on outdoor furniture, cars, soil and crops.
Residents in the projected plume path were advised to shelter indoors with their pets, shut windows, and limit exposure to outdoor air during a precautionary period, pending the Army’s all-clear.
Those living near Middletown City Park and Butterfly Park were also instructed to leave their homes for six hours to avoid ground vibrations that could crack or shatter nearby windows.
In the plume’s aftermath, the Army said residents would need to hose down outdoor surfaces, vehicles, and play equipment in an effort to flush away any lead dust deposited during the detonation.
But experts have expressed doubt about how practical the safety guidance is.
At a news briefing, University of Iowa professor David Cwiertny, the director of the Center for Health Effects of Environmental Contamination, warned that long-term monitoring would be necessary to track the lead’s distribution.
“We know that, unlike a porch or patio table, you cannot simply wipe down farm fields, gardens or topsoil because those surfaces are hard to clean,” Cwiertny said.
“We will ultimately need to rely on actual field samples after the event to measure how much lead settles there and understand what it means for our land, those crops and the quality of the environment.”
The Army has yet to issue revised instructions or specify new evacuation hours following the delayed detonation.
Earthjustice lawyers like Chau say the lack of communication is part of the problem.
“The way they’ve gone about notifying people and claiming that they’re going to clean things up when they don’t even know the extent of impact, that is extremely concerning,” Chau told Al Jazeera.
Weather concerns?
US Representative Eric Sorensen, the only meteorologist serving in Congress, said the Army should be looking at a window of opportunity that presents the least potential for off-site exposure.
In a video posted on Thursday, Sorensen said, “The most optimum conditions for controlled detonation would be when we have an inversion of clouds, warm air over cool, with light winds.”
He warned that the National Weather Service’s forecast does not offer those favourable conditions over the coming week, and he questioned why the detonations were only announced when cold weather was imminent.
Other questions remain about whether the Army has exhausted every practicable means of containing the lead’s spread.
Bruce Lanphear, a paediatric epidemiologist and professor of health sciences at Simon Fraser University, told Al Jazeera that it should be up to the Army to provide credible estimates of airborne lead concentrations, ground-level deposition and exposure levels before taking action.
“The burden should be on them to demonstrate that this is the least harmful option, not merely the fastest way to eliminate an immediate danger,” Lanphear told Al Jazeera.

title: Poland says Russia tried to assassinate Ukrainian rapper twice
text:
Poland says Russia tried to assassinate Ukrainian rapper twice
Polish confirmation comes after Copenhagen reveals alleged Russian plot to kill US-Ukrainian citizen on Danish soil.
Polish authorities have said Russian intelligence services tried to kill a Ukrainian-American rapper visiting the country in August, after Copenhagen said Moscow had allegedly targeted the same man on Danish soil.
The alleged assassination plan targeted Albert Vasiliev, a rapper who performs under the name Kyivstoner and holds Ukrainian and US citizenship, according to Danish media.
Polish Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesman Maciej Wewior confirmed the alleged plot to kill Vasiliev in Poland to The Associated Press news agency on Sunday.
On Friday, in response to Denmark’s statement about the alleged assassination plan, Poland’s Foreign Ministry had written, “It is the second assassination attempt against the same person. The first one was foiled on the Polish territory in August 2026.”
It also said that a Russian national had been arrested.
Polish authorities detained the suspect, who was allegedly recruited by Moscow, on August 7.
Denmark announced the expulsion of a Russian diplomat on Friday after it accused Moscow intelligence of plotting the assassination during a concert in a Copenhagen suburb in September.
Denmark’s intelligence agency, PET, said on the same day that it suspected Russia of planning the assassination with the help of a banned Danish gang.
Two Danish men appeared in court near Copenhagen on Friday, charged with assisting a foreign intelligence service and attempted murder.
Russia dismissed the allegations through its embassy in Copenhagen, saying they were unsubstantiated.
Previously, on August 13, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk disclosed that a plot to kill a Ukrainian-American in Warsaw was thwarted. He did not disclose Vasiliev’s name at the time but said the target “was uncomfortable” for Russian President Vladimir Putin’s government.
Support for Ukraine
Vasiliev has expressed his support for Ukraine amid Russia’s ongoing war on the country and was performing across Europe this year before his concerts were cancelled for security reasons.
Russia’s domestic security service, the FSB, accused Vasiliev of being involved in supplying drones for an alleged Ukrainian attack on a defence enterprise in the Moscow region. It said he was “acting under the patronage” of Ukraine’s internal security service, the SBU.
Danish broadcaster DR reported that Vasiliev denied the FSB accusations.
Danish Minister for Foreign Affairs Lars Lokke Rasmussen told reporters on Friday that Denmark was also considering suspending Schengen visas for Russians.
Poland’s Foreign Ministry said it backed the move.
“Poland supports measures Denmark suggested to limit the access and freedom of travel of Russian nationals on the EU territory,” it said on X.
Western officials have accused Russia and its proxies of staging dozens of attacks and other incidents across Europe since Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Russia has denied those accusations.

title: WHO chief calls for peace amid heavy fighting in Ebola-hit DR Congo region
text:
WHO chief calls for peace amid heavy fighting in Ebola-hit DR Congo region
Fighting near DRC hospital disrupts Ebola efforts, putting patients and workers at ‘grave risk’, WHO warns.
The World Health Organization (WHO) chief has urged peace following heavy fighting in the Democratic Republic of the Congo’s (DRC) northeastern province, the epicentre of the Ebola outbreak.
WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said on Sunday that fighting near a hospital in the DRC’s Ituri province disrupted Ebola response efforts and forced health workers and aid partners to shelter inside a maternity ward for more than 24 hours.
“Heavy fighting has been ongoing since yesterday in the vicinity of a hospital in Ituri – in an area close to where the Ebola outbreak first emerged,” Tedros said on X.
“The situation has disrupted the work of the hospital and the wider Ebola response, putting patients, families and health workers at grave risk.”
Medical staff have been sheltering for their lives in a maternity ward in the facility for more than 24 hours, and the WHO is working to arrange a safe exit for the team and “for the hospital facilities, staff and patients to be protected,” Tedros also said.
“The best medicine is peace,” he added.
‘High-level transmission continues’
As of November 17, the WHO reported a total of 5,678 deaths out of 11,613 cases in the DRC, the largest and deadliest Ebola outbreak in the country.
The WHO said in a statement on Saturday that “while some areas had seen a slight decline in cases, sustained, high-level transmission continues overall in the country.”
Ituri and North Kivu, in the eastern part of the DRC, remain the most affected provinces.
The virus, which is transmitted through contact with bodily fluids, has spread across swaths of the DRC’s east and northeast, which have been plagued by violence for more than 30 years.
Earlier in November, armed men thought to be linked to an ISIL (ISIS)-affiliated group raided villages and killed dozens of people in North Kivu, forcing patients with confirmed and suspected Ebola infections to flee.
The outbreak is also occurring amid ongoing fighting between government forces and the Rwanda-backed M23 armed group, which has seized key cities in eastern DRC, making transport of healthcare resources to remote regions difficult.

title: Asian stock markets tumble as AI bubble fears mount
text:
Asian stock markets tumble as AI bubble fears mount
Stocks fall in South Korea, Taiwan, mainland China and Hong Kong as tech sell-off deepens.
Asian stock markets have opened to sharp losses amid persistent concerns over the sustainability of the AI boom.
Markets in South Korea, Hong Kong and mainland China sank deeper into the red on Monday, continuing Friday’s tech-led sell-off on both sides of the Pacific.
The Korea Composite Stock Price Index (Kospi) in Seoul slid as much as 5.8 percent, before paring some losses in the afternoon.
The index, which includes memory chip giants Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, was down 3.2 percent as of 04:30 GMT.
Hong Kong’s Hang Seng Index and the CSI 300 Index in Shanghai were both down about 0.6 percent, after falling nearly 2 percent and 1.3 percent, respectively, in morning trading.
After opening lower, the Taiwan Stock Exchange Capitalization Weighted Stock Index (Taiex) in Taipei rebounded to gain 2.5 percent.
Japan’s stock markets were closed for Labour Thanksgiving Day.
Following Friday’s rout in Asia, Wall Street’s benchmark S&P 500 closed 3.7 percent lower to enter a correction – the term investors use when the market drops 10 percent or more from its recent high.
The tech-focused Nasdaq Composite, roughly half of which is made up of the “Magnificent Seven” AI-oriented firms, dropped 5.3 percent to erase all of its gains for 2026.
The Kospi, Nikkei 225, and the Taiex entered the weekend between 5.1 percent and 6.2 percent lower, while the Hang Seng Index finished down 1.9 percent.
Wall Street appeared on track for a strong rebound on Monday, with S&P 500 and Nasdaq futures up 2.2 percent and 2.9 percent, respectively.
After last week’s losses, investors are trying to assess if the market correction has “gone too far”, said Rajat Agarwal, an Asia equity strategist with Societe Generale.
“I think markets are trying to find some ground after a massive sell-off in [the] US on Friday, a more than a three-standard-deviation event in tech indices,” Agarwal told Al Jazeera.
Investors have long been concerned that tech firms may not be able to sustain the multi-trillion-dollar investments they have poured into the infrastructure needed to train and run AI.
Global AI-related investment is expected to reach $2.7 trillion in 2026 and $3.6 trillion in 2027, according to technology insights company Gartner.
The debt-fuelled investment splurge has stirred intense debate about whether tech firms are creating a stock market bubble similar to the one that emerged in the run-up to the 2000 dot-com crash
Concerns that the AI boom may be running out of steam have been exacerbated by growing calls for greater oversight of the sector.
The Democratic Party’s sweeping victory in the US midterm elections is expected to slow data centre construction in US states, while the alleged espionage scandal embroiling chip giant Nvidia and its former CEO Jensen Huang has led to a push for tighter restrictions on China’s access to advanced chips.
“AI-related concerns will continue to dominate this week, as investors try to determine if the bottom is near,” Khoon Goh, head of Asia research at ANZ, told Al Jazeera.
“A bright spot is that US equity futures are up, and South Korea reported very strong exports for the first 20 days of November, driven by semiconductor exports, which are up 294.4 percent year-on-year,” Goh said.

title: Cameroon’s ex-rebels caught between hiding and broken promises
text:
Cameroon’s ex-rebels caught between hiding and broken promises
Cameroon’s former rebels face arrest fears and failed reintegration.
Douala, Cameroon – Collins Mbah says he hunted down and killed several Cameroonian soldiers in the English-speaking Northwest region during his time as a separatist fighter between 2016 and 2020. Today, in the coastal city of Douala, the man in his mid-30s, who went by the name Commander No Sorrow, has taken on a different role: traditional healer, tending to lives rather than taking them.
Mbah says he abandoned the armed struggle after realising that fellow fighters were turning against the very people they had set out to protect. But he has firmly ruled out joining the government’s disarmament, demobilisation and reintegration (DDR) programme.
“Quitting the struggle and joining the government disarmament programme would have meant I betrayed the people,” said Mbah, who dropped out of secondary school to join the revolt. “I don’t want to have anything to do with the government or the struggle any more. All I need now is peace of mind,” he told Al Jazeera.
October marked a decade since protests erupted in Cameroon’s English-speaking Northwest and Southwest regions, eventually escalating into an armed conflict between separatist fighters and government forces.
The unrest began in late 2016 after Anglophone lawyers and teachers protested against the appointment of Francophone magistrates unfamiliar with British common law to courts in English-speaking regions, and French-speaking teachers unable to communicate fluently in English to schools there. The protests were met with a government crackdown and eventually gave rise to a separatist movement seeking independence for the two regions, which its supporters call “Ambazonia”.
The conflict has killed thousands of people, displaced hundreds of thousands and disrupted education across the two English-speaking regions, according to humanitarian and human rights organisations. New figures released in October by the Cameroonian nonprofit Centre for Human Rights and Democracy in Africa (CHRDA) suggest the death toll could be as high as 10,000.
The fighting remains deadlocked, with separatist groups continuing attacks and kidnappings while the government pursues a military campaign. Alongside its military operations, the government has launched a community dialogue initiative, after distancing itself from Swiss- and Canadian-supported peace efforts.
Prime Minister Joseph Dion Ngute launched the initiative in Buea, the capital of Southwest, in September and in Bamenda, the capital of the Northwest, on October 15. Local leaders are being encouraged to persuade fighters to surrender and enter DDR centres. At the two events, 55 fighters – 25 in the Southwest and 30 in the Northwest – were presented as having renounced the armed struggle.
Life beyond the battlefield
Despite leaving the rebellion, Mbah says he remains on the government’s wanted list. Without a national identity card, the father of three struggles to move freely around Douala and occasionally ventures into the outskirts to collect traditional herbs.
“I was initiated into traditional healing during childhood. The amulets and concoctions helped me foresee any danger when I was on the war front. Today, I use the same to heal,” he said. “But I don’t stay in a particular neighbourhood for long – I always move to the next to avoid being caught.”
Mbah is among former fighters who have chosen to reintegrate into society independently rather than enter government-run rehabilitation centres. Many say they fear arrest or poor treatment if they surrender.
Peter Mosongo, 28, now works as a motorcycle taxi rider in Buea after leaving the struggle in 2019. He joined in 2018 to protect his family but quit after witnessing what he describes as the indiscriminate killing of civilians by fellow fighters.
“I received threats from the fighters when I quit. They even kidnapped my father to force him to produce me,” Mosongo said. “I didn’t join DDR upon quitting out of fear that I may end up in prison. It was also being rumoured that those who surrendered were being killed silently.”
Mosongo says he also lost two cousins to the conflict.
Another former fighter, Richard Bende, left in 2019 because he believed the rebellion had become a “scores-settling venture”. He had fought government soldiers in Bamusso, in the Southwest, and now works as a secondary school history and geography teacher. Like Mbah and Mosongo, he avoided the DDR programme, citing concerns about the treatment of former fighters at its centres.
Broken promises inside DDR centres
Paul Mukete, who fought in Kumba from 2017 to 2020 under the nickname King of Vultures, chose a different path. But six years after entering the DDR programme in Tiko town, in the Southwest, he says he has little to show for it.
Apart from learning poultry and pig farming, Mukete says he has received no psychological care.
“We gave intelligence information to the military, who used it to kill some separatist fighters who refused to lay down their weapons,” he said. “We were about 600 in the DDR centre, but many have since left out of frustration. Some even rejoined the struggle and got killed.”
The 29-year-old father of three now takes on odd jobs to support his family.
His account raises questions about whether the programme is providing former fighters with the support they need to rebuild their lives and remain out of the conflict.
Fonbeh Hedwick Chia, a mental health specialist and founder of the Bamenda-based Living Vine Mental Health Services, says both fighters and civilians in the English-speaking regions have been exposed to psychological trauma.
He argues that the DDR centres lack the therapeutic support needed to rehabilitate former fighters, estimating that about 800 have renounced the armed struggle.
“The government is more concerned with the propaganda made when they come to the DDR than their integral welfare,” Chia told Al Jazeera, arguing that former fighters need psychological care to address the trauma of atrocities committed and witnessed during the conflict.
Without proper rehabilitation, he warns, former fighters risk remaining marginalised and could become a source of further instability.
The accounts of former fighters and Chia’s assessment point to a central challenge for the DDR programme: persuading rebels to surrender is only the first step, while helping them return to civilian life requires sustained support.
A conflict rooted in colonial history
Cameroon’s Anglophone crisis has roots in its colonial past. Initially colonised by Germany in 1884, the territory was divided between Britain and France after World War I.
French Cameroon gained independence in 1960. In 1961, British-administered Southern Cameroons voted in a United Nations-organised plebiscite to join the independent Republic of Cameroon, forming a federal state. The arrangement was dissolved in 1972 following a controversial referendum, ending the Anglophone regions’ federal status.
Unlike some conflicts involving more centralised rebel movements, Cameroon’s separatist rebellion has no single command structure. Dozens of smaller factions operate across Northwest and Southwest, with some receiving financial support and weapons from diaspora groups.
The prolonged fighting has brought human rights abuses by both government forces and separatists. Some armed groups have also shifted towards criminal activities, including kidnapping for ransom.
Chris Roberts, a political scientist at the University of Calgary in Canada, says the conflict is rooted less in language differences than in “decades of poor governance from a political system that has kept the same president in power since 1982”.
Although the government has repeatedly claimed the war is over, Roberts says continued firefights, ambushes and attacks demonstrate otherwise.
He argues that political reform in Yaoundé is essential to ending the conflict. He describes the October 2025 presidential election as “strategically rigged” and argues that it offers little prospect of resolving the crisis. A future presidential succession crisis could create opportunities for reform but also risk destabilising the country.
“There will not be a military solution to this war,” Roberts said.
